sourceDefinition: [lit.] He (an ass) became a she-ass. (M.) The saying, kaAna HimaAr~aA faAsotaA^otana , said of a man, [lit.] signifies [ He was a he ass, ] and he became a she ass; meaning (assumed tropical:) he was mighty, or of high condition, [like the wild he-ass,] and he became base, abject, or vile. (S, TA.) ― -b2- Also, (S, TA,) or AstA^tn A^ataAn~aA , (M,) He (a man) purchased a she-ass; (S;) he took for himself a she-ass. (S, M.)

And A^ataAnu Alv~amiyli signifies A large mass of rock in the interior of the water-course, which nothing raises or moves, of the measure of the stature of a man in length and likewise in breadth. sourceDefinition: (T, M, Mgh, Msb, K) and A^at~uwnN , (K,) or, accord. to J, (Msb,) it is thus, with teshdeed, but pronounced without teshdeed by the vulgar, (S, Msb,) A certain place in which fire is kindled, (S, Mgh,) called in Persian kulaxon [or kuloxano ], pertaining to a bath: and metaphorically applied to (tropical:) that in which bricks are baked, and called in Persian tuwnaqo and daA$uwzano [or simply tuwno and daA$o ]: (Mgh:) accord. to Az, (Msb,) it is that of the bath, and of the place in which gypsum is made: (T, Msb:) or the trench, hollow, or pit, of the jay~aAra [or lime-burner, (in the CK, erroneously, the xab~Az ,]) and of the preparer of gypsum; (M, K, TA;) and the like: (K:) the pl. [said in the TA to be of the latter, but it is implied in the T and M and Mgh that it is of the former,] is A^ataAtiynu , (T, S, M, Mgh, Msb, K, [in the CK, erroneously, AatAniyonu ,]) by common consent of the Arabs, (Mgh,) with two t s, (T,) accord. to Fr, who says that they sometimes double a letter in the pl. when they do not double it in the sing., (T,) and accord. to IJ, who says that it seems as though they changed A^atuwnN to A^at~uwnN ; (M;) and [of A^atuwnN , as is said in the TA and implied in the M,] A^utunN . (M, K.) [J says that] it is said to be post-classical; (S;) [and ISd says,] I do not think it to be Arabic. (M.)

definition: [The plum; ] a certain fruit, (K, TA,) of the description termed faAkihap , (TA,) well known; (Msb, K;) cold and moist; or, as some say, of moderate temperature; (TA;) which facilitates the flow of...
sourceDefinition: [The plum; ] a certain fruit, (K, TA,) of the description termed faAkihap , (TA,) well known; (Msb, K;) cold and moist; or, as some say, of moderate temperature; (TA;) which facilitates the flow of the yellow bile; (K;) i. e., its juice, or water, does so, when drunk with sugar-candy ( Tabaroza* ) and manna ( taranojubiyn ) added to it; (TA;) and allays thirst, and heat of the heart; (K;) but it relaxes the stomach, and does not agree with it; and it generates a watery mixture; and its injurious effect is repelled by the drinking of sugary sikanojubiyn [or oxymel ]: it is of several kinds: (TA:) [ the most common is the Damasc, or Damascene, plum: ] the best is (K, TA) the Armenian, (TA,) that which is sweet and large: (K, TA:) the sour, or acid, is less laxative, and more cold: (TA:) the n. un. is with p : (S, Msb, K:) you should not say A_inojaASN ; (Yaakoob, S, K;) or this is a word of weak authority, (K, TA,) and you say A_ij~aASN and A_injaASN like as one says A_ij~aArN and A_inojaArN : (TA:) in the dial. of the Syrians, the A_ij~aASN [or A_inojaAS or A_injaAs accord. to common modern usage among them] is the [ pear which they formerly called] mi$omi$ and [which others call] kum~avoray : (K:) it is of the growth of the country of the Arabs: (AHn:) Aj~AS is an adventitious word, (S, K,) or arabicized, (Msb,) because j and S do not both occur in any Arabic word: (S, Msb, K:) or, accord. to Az, they do so occur; as, for instance, in HaS~aSa , and in Saj~N . (TA.)

definition: , (S, M, A, K,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, M, A, K,) aor. , (K,) inf. n. A^asadN , (TA,) (tropical:) He (a man, M) was, or became, like a lion, (S, M, A, K,) in his boldness, (A,) and his other dispositions; (S, A, TA;) as also ↓ AstA^sd ; (M, A, K;) [and ↓ tA^s~d ; (see A^asidN ;)] Ealayohi towards him, or against him. (A.) You say A^asadN bay~inu AlA^asadi [ A lion bearing evidence of being like a lion in boldness ]: an extr. phrase, like Hiq~apN bayin~apN AlH~iqapi ; (TA;) which is [said to be] the only other instance of the kind. (TA in art. Hq .) [Hence the saying,] A_i*aA daxala fahida wa A_i*aA xaraja A^asida (tropical:) [ When he comes in, he is like a lynx; and when he goes out, he is like a lion: see fahida ]. (S, from a trad.) You say also, A^asida Ealayohi meaning (assumed tropical:) He became emboldened against him; (TA;) as also ↓ AstA^sd . (S, Msb, K.) And (assumed tropical:) He was, or became, angry with him: (M, L, K: *) or (so accord. to the M and L, but in the K, “ and,”) behaved in a light and hasty manner, or foolishly, or ignorantly, towards him. (M, L, K.*) ― -b2- A^asida , (S, K,) aor. as above, (K,) and so the inf. n., (TA,) also signifies (assumed tropical:) He (a man, S) became stupified (S, K) by fear (S) at seeing a lion. (S, K.) Thus it has two contr. meanings. (K.) -A2- A^asada , aor. , i. q. sabaEa [(assumed tropical:) He bit another with his teeth, like as does the beast of prey: or he reviled, vilified, or vituperated, another; charged him with a vice or fault or the like; or assailed him with foul language, such as displeased him]. (K.) ― -b2- See also 4.

sourceDefinition: , (T, S, M, Msb, K,) aor. , (S, Msb, K,) inf. n. A_ilufN (S, M, Msb, K) and A^alofN (K) and A_ilaAfN and wilaAfN , which is anomalous, and A^alafaAnN , (M, TA,) He kept, or clave, to it; (A'Obeyd, T, M, Msb, * TA;) namely, a thing, (A'Obeyd, T, M, TA,) or a place; (S, Msb, TA;) as also A^alafahu , aor. ; (TA;) and ↓ A=lfhu , (A'Obeyd, T, S, M, Msb,) aor. yuw^olifu (S, TA,) inf. n. A_iylaAfN ; (S, Msb, TA;) and ↓ A=lfhu , aor. yuw^aAlifu , inf. n. muw^aAlafapN and A_ilaAfN : (S, Msb, TA:) [ he frequented it, or resorted to it habitually; namely, a place:] he became familiar with it; or accustomed, or habituated, to it; namely, a thing: (AZ, T:) he became familiar, sociable, companionable, friendly, or amicable, with him: (AZ, T, Msb:) he loved, or affected, him; liked, approved, or took pleasure in, him. (Msb.) You say, A^alifati AlT~ayoru AlHarama [ The birds kept to the sacred territory ], and Albuyuwta [ the houses ]: and AlZ~ibaA='u Alr~amoli ↓ A=lafati The gazelles kept to the sands. (T.) ― -b2- There are three manners of reading the passage in the Kur [evi. 1 and 2], qurayo$K A_iylaAfihimo riHolapa Al$~itaA='i wa AlS~ayofi ↓ liA_iylaAfi ; the second and third being liA_ilaAfi and liA_ilofi ; the first and second of which have been adopted; (Aboo-Is-hák, T, TA;) and the third also; this being the reading of the Prophet [himself]: (TA:) [accord. to all these readings, the passage may be rendered, For the keeping of Kureysh, for their keeping to the journey of the winter and of the summer, or spring; the chapter going on to say, for this reason "let them worship the Lord of this House," &c. : or] the second and third readings are from A^alifa , aor. yaA^olafu ; [and accord. to these readings, the passage may be rendered as above;] but accord. to the first reading, the meaning is, for the preparing and fitting out [&c.; i. e., preparing and fitting out men and beasts in the journey of the winter &c.]: so says IAmb; and Fr explains in the same manner the third reading: but IAar says that, accord. to this reading, the meaning is, the protecting [&c.]: he says that the persons who protected were four brothers, Háshim and 'Abd-Shems and El-Muttalib and Nowfal, the sons of 'Abd-Menáf: these gave protection to Kureysh in their procuring of corn: (T:) Háshim obtained a grant of security from the king of the Greeks, and Nowfal from Kisrà, and 'Abd-Shems from the Nejáshee, and ElMuttalib from the kings of Himyer; and the merchants of Kureysh used to go to and from the great towns of these kings with the grants of security of these brothers, and none opposed them: Háshim used to give protection ( yuw^olifu [in the copies of the K yuw^al~ifu ]) [to those journeying] to Syria, and 'Abd-Shems to Abyssinia, and ElMuttalib to El-Yemen, and Nowfal to Persia: (T, K: *) or ↓ A_iylaAf in the Kur signifies a covenant, or an obligation; and what resembles permission, ( A_ijaAzap , as in some copies of the K and in the TA,) or protection, ( A_ijaArap , as in the CK,) with an obligation involving responsibility for safety; first obtained by Háshim, from the kings of Syria; (K, * TA;) and the explanation is, that Kureysh were dwelling in the sacred territory, (K,) having neither seed-produce nor udders [to yield them milk], (TA,) secure in the procuring of their provisions from other parts, and in their changes of place, in winter and summer, or spring; the people around them having their property seized; whereas, when any cause of mischief occurred to them, they said, "We are people of the sacred territory," and then no one opposed them: (K:) so in the O: (TA:) or the l is to denote wonder; and the meaning is, wonder ye at the AylAf of Kureysh [&c.]: (K:) some say that the meaning is connected with what follows; i. e., let them worship the Lord of this House for the AylAf [&c., agreeably with the first explanation which we have given]: others, that it is connected with what precedes; as J says; (TA;) the meaning being, I have destroyed the masters of the elephant to make Kureysh remain at Mekkeh, and for their uniting the journey of the winter and of the summer, or spring; that when they finished one, they should commence the other; (T, S;) and this is like the saying, Darabotuhu lika*aA Darabotuhu lika*aA a lika*aA , with suppression of the [conjunctive] w : (S:) but Ibn-'Arafeh disapproves of this, for two reasons: first, because the phrase "In the name of God" &c. occurs between the two chapters: [Bd, however, mentions that in Ubeí's copy, the two compose one chapter:] secondly, because AylAf signifies the covenants, or obligations, which they obtained when they went forth on mercantile expeditions, and whereby they became secure. (TA.) ↓ A_ilaAfN [in like manner] signifies A writing of security, written by the king for people, that they may be secure in his territory: and is used by Musáwir Ibn-Hind in the sense of AiytilaAfN [as is also A_ilofN ,] when he says, in satirizing Benoo-Asad, zaEamotumo A^an~a A_ixowatakumo qurayo$N lahumo A_ilofN wa layosa lakumo A_ilaAfu meaning Ye asserted [that your brothers are Kureysh; i. e.,] that ye are like Kureysh: but how should ye be like them? for they have [an alliance whereby they are protected in ] the trade of El-Yemen and Syria; and ye have not that [ alliance ]. (Ham p. 636.) [Hence,] A_ilaAfu A@ll~`hi [a phrase used in the manner of an oath,] accord. to some, signifies The safeguard, or protection, of God: or, accord. to others, an honourable station from God. (TA.) -A2- A^alafahu , aor. , He gave him a thousand; (S, K) of articles of property, and of camels. (TA.)

(Msb.) You say, A^alifati AlT~ayoru AlHarama [ The birds kept to the sacred territory ], and Albuyuwta [ the houses ]: and AlZ~ibaA='u Alr~amoli ↓ A=lafati The gazelles kept to the sands. (T.) ― -b2- There are three manners of reading the passage in the Kur [evi. 1 and 2], qurayo$K A_iylaAfihimo riHolapa Al$~itaA='i wa AlS~ayofi ↓ liA_iylaAfi ; the second and third being liA_ilaAfi and liA_ilofi ; the first and second of which have been adopted; (Aboo-Is-hák, T, TA;) and the third also; this being the reading of the Prophet [himself]: (TA:) [accord. to all these readings, the passage may be rendered, For the keeping of Kureysh, for their keeping to the journey of the winter and of the summer, or spring; the chapter going on to say, for this reason "let them worship the Lord of this House," &c. : or] the second and third readings are from A^alifa , aor. yaA^olafu ; [and accord. to these readings, the passage may be rendered as above;] but accord. to the first reading, the meaning is, for the preparing and fitting out [&c.; i. e., preparing and fitting out men and beasts in the journey of the winter &c.]: so says IAmb; and Fr explains in the same manner the third reading: but IAar says that, accord. to this reading, the meaning is, the protecting [&c.]: he says that the persons who protected were four brothers, Háshim and 'Abd-Shems and El-Muttalib and Nowfal, the sons of 'Abd-Menáf: these gave protection to Kureysh in their procuring of corn: (T:) Háshim obtained a grant of security from the king of the Greeks, and Nowfal from Kisrà, and 'Abd-Shems from the Nejáshee, and ElMuttalib from the kings of Himyer; and the merchants of Kureysh used to go to and from the great towns of these kings with the grants of security of these brothers, and none opposed them: Háshim used to give protection ( yuw^olifu [in the copies of the K yuw^al~ifu ]) [to those journeying] to Syria, and 'Abd-Shems to Abyssinia, and ElMuttalib to El-Yemen, and Nowfal to Persia: (T, K: *) or ↓ A_iylaAf in the Kur signifies a covenant, or an obligation; and what resembles permission, ( A_ijaAzap , as in some copies of the K and in the TA,) or protection, ( A_ijaArap , as in the CK,) with an obligation involving responsibility for safety; first obtained by Háshim, from the kings of Syria; (K, * TA;) and the explanation is, that Kureysh were dwelling in the sacred territory, (K,) having neither seed-produce nor udders [to yield them milk], (TA,) secure in the procuring of their provisions from other parts, and in their changes of place, in winter and summer, or spring; the people around them having their property seized; whereas, when any cause of mischief occurred to them, they said, "We are people of the sacred territory," and then no one opposed them: (K:) so in the O: (TA:) or the l is to denote wonder; and the meaning is, wonder ye at the AylAf of Kureysh [&c.]: (K:) some say that the meaning is connected with what follows; i. e., let them worship the Lord of this House for the AylAf [&c., agreeably with the first explanation which we have given]: others, that it is connected with what precedes; as J says; (TA;) the meaning being, I have destroyed the masters of the elephant to make Kureysh remain at Mekkeh, and for their uniting the journey of the winter and of the summer, or spring; that when they finished one, they should commence the other; (T, S;) and this is like the saying, Darabotuhu lika*aA Darabotuhu lika*aA a lika*aA , with suppression of the [conjunctive] w : (S:) but Ibn-'Arafeh disapproves of this, for two reasons: first, because the phrase "In the name of God" &c. occurs between the two chapters: [Bd, however, mentions that in Ubeí's copy, the two compose one chapter:] secondly, because AylAf signifies the covenants, or obligations, which they obtained when they went forth on mercantile expeditions, and whereby they became secure. (TA.) ↓ A_ilaAfN [in like manner] signifies A writing of security, written by the king for people, that they may be secure in his territory: and is used by Musáwir Ibn-Hind in the sense of AiytilaAfN [as is also A_ilofN ,] when he says, in satirizing Benoo-Asad, zaEamotumo A^an~a A_ixowatakumo qurayo$N lahumo A_ilofN wa layosa lakumo A_ilaAfu meaning Ye asserted [that your brothers are Kureysh; i. e.,] that ye are like Kureysh: but how should ye be like them? for they have [an alliance whereby they are protected in ] the trade of El-Yemen and Syria; and ye have not that [ alliance ]. (Ham p. 636.) [Hence,] A_ilaAfu A@ll~`hi [a phrase used in the manner of an oath,] accord. to some, signifies The safeguard, or protection, of God: or, accord. to others, an honourable station from God. (TA.) -A2- A^alafahu , aor. , He gave him a thousand; (S, K) of articles of property, and of camels. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , inf. n. taA^oliyfN , (T, Msb, K,) He united them, or brought them together, (T, Msb, TA,) after separation; (T, TA;) and made them to love one another; (Msb;) he caused union, or companionship, ( A^ulofap ,) to take place between them. (K.) And A^al~afotu bayona Al$~ayoy^ayoni , inf. n. as above, [ I united, or put together, the two things. ] (S.) (T, M.) ― -b2- Hence, taA^oliyfu Alkutubi [ The composition of books ]. (T, TA.) ― -b3- taA^oliyfN is The putting many things into such a state that one name becomes applicable to them, whether there be to some of the parts a relation to others by precedence and sequence, or not: so that it is a more general term than tarotiybN : (KT:) or the collecting together, or putting together, suitable things; from AlAlfp [i. e. AlA^ulofapu ]; and is a more particular term than tarokiybN , which is the putting together things, whether suitable or not, or placed in order or not. (Kull p. 118.) -A2- A^al~afuwA A_ilaY ka*aA : see 5. -A3- A^l~f A^alifFA He wrote an alif; (K;) like as one says jay~ama jiymFA . (TA.) -A4- See also 4, in three places.

sourceDefinition: [originally an inf. n. of A^alifahu , q. v.,] He with whom one is familiar, sociable, companionable, friendly, or amicable; he to whom one keeps or cleaves; [ a constant companion or associate; a mate; a fellow; a yoke-fellow; one who is familiar, &c., with another or others; (see muw^al~afN ;)] (M;) i. q. ↓ A^aliyfN ; (T, S, M, K;) which is an act. part. n. of A^alifahu ; (Msb;) as is also ↓ A=lifN ; (Msb, K;) and ↓ A^alifN also is syn. with A^aliyfN : (K:) the female is termed A_ilofapN and A_ilofN ; (M;) both of these signifying a woman with whom thou art familiar, &c., and who is familiar, &c., with thee: (K:) and the fem. of ↓ A=lifN is A=lifapN : (K:) the pl. of A_ilofN is A=laAfN ; (T, M;) which is also pl. of ↓ A^alifN : (TA:) and that of ↓ A^aliyfN is A^alaAy^ifu (S, K, TA) and A^ulafaA='u : (M, TA:) and that of ↓ A=lifN is A^ul~aAfN (T, S, Msb, K) and A=laAfN , like as A^anoSaArN is pl. of naASirN , (TA,) and so, (M, TA,) in my opinion, [says ISd,] (M,) is A^uluwfN , like as $uhuwdN is pl. of $aAhidN , (M, TA,) though some say that it is pl. of A_ilofN : (M:) and the pl. of ↓ A=lifapN is A^awaAlifu and A=lifaAtN . (K.) You say, fvlaAnN A_ilofiY and ↓ A^aliyfiY [ Such a one is my constant companion or associate, &c.] (T.) And Han~ati AlA_ilofu A_ilaY A_ilofi [ The female mate yearned towards the mate ]. (S.) A^uluwfN in the Kur ii. 244 is said by some to be pl. of A_ilofN or of ↓ A=lifN : but by others, to signify "thousands." (Bd, L, TA.) AlT~ayori ↓ A^awaAlifu signifies The birds that keep to Mekkeh and the sacred territory: and AlHamaAmi ↓ A^awaAlifu Domestic pigeons. (T.)

definition: and ↓ maA^oluwfN Kept to, or clove to;
sourceDefinition: and ↓ maA^oluwfN Kept to, or clove to; applied to a thing [and to a person; and meaning when applied to the latter, with whom one is familiar, sociable, &c.]. (T.) It is said in a trad., Almuw^ominu ↓ A_ilofN maA^oluwfN [ The believer is one who is familiar, or sociable, &c., with others, and with whom others are familiar, &c.]. (TA.) ― -b2- Almuw^al~afapu quluwbuhumo Those whose hearts are made to incline, or are conciliated, by beneficence and love or affection: (S, * Msb:) as used in the Kur [ix. 60], it is applied to certain chief persons of the Arabs, whom the Prophet was commanded to attract, or allure, and to present with gifts, (T, K,) from the poor-rates, (TA,) in order that they might make those after them desirous of becoming Muslims, (T, K,) and lest care for things which they deemed sacred, or inviolable, together with the weakness of their intentions, should induce them to combine in hostility with the unbelievers against the Muslims; for which purpose, he gave them, on the day of Honeyn, eighty [in the TA two hundred ] camels: (T:) they were certain men of eminence, of the Arabs, to whom the Prophet used to give gifts from the poor-rates; to some of them, to prevent their acting injuriously; and to some, from a desire of their becoming Muslims, (Mgh, Msb,) and their followers also; (Msb;) and to some, in order that they might remain stedfast as Muslims, because of their having recently become such; but when Aboo-Bekr became appointed to the government, he forbade this practice. (Mgh, Msb.) -A2- A^alofN muw^al~afapN [These are a thousand ] made complete. (S.) ― -b2- See also mw^lfwn .

Abw ]; (S;) the current phrase of the Arabs being that which includes both parents: (TA:) i. e., a man said so to another man, (Lth, T, M,) or to a child; (Fr, S, M;) and in like manner to his horse, for having saved him from some accident: (IAar, T:) the verb is derived from biA^abiY . (Lth, T, M.) Hence AlbiA^abo , in an ex. cited voce A^abN , in art. Abw , q. v.; (M;) or Albiy^abo ; (TA in art. Abw ;) or Albiyabo . (S in that art.) ― -b2- And [hence,] baA^baw^uwhu They made a show of treating him with graciousness, courtesy, or blandishment; as also Ealayohi ↓ tabaA^obaw^uwA . (M.) ― -b3- [Hence also,] ↓ baA^obaA='N , with medd, [used as an inf. n.,] A woman's dandling, or dancing, of her child. (AA, T.) -A2- baA^obaA^a also signifies He (a child) said ↓ baA^obaA^o (M, K) [in some copies of the K written baAbaA , both meaning Papa, or Father, ] to his father. (M.) [Accord. to the TA, the verb is trans. in this sense, as in the senses before explained; but I think that baA^obaA^ahu has been there erroneously put for baA^obaA^a .] ― -b2- And He (a stallion [meaning a stallion-camel]) reiterated the sound of the letter b [or b ] in his braying. (M.) ― -b3- [And hence, perhaps,] ↓ baA^obaA^N [or, more probably, ↓ baA^obaA='N , with medd, agreeably with analogy, used as an inf. n.,] The chiding of the cat, or act of chiding the cat; (AA, T, Sgh;) also termed gas~N . (AA, T.) -A3- Also He hastened, made haste, or sped: and ↓ tabaA^obaA^onaA we hastened, &c.: (marginal note in a copy of the S:) or ↓ tabaA^obaA^a signifies he ran. (ElUmawee, T, K.)

definition: The source, origin, race, root, or stock, syn.
sourceDefinition: The source, origin, race, root, or stock, syn. A^aSolN , (AA, Sh, T, S, M, K,) of a man, (Sh, T,) whether noble or base. (AA, T.) You say, huwa kariymu Albuw^obuw^i He is of generous, or noble, origin; lit., generous, or noble, of origin. (TK.) And fulaAnN fiYbuw^obuw^i Alkarami Such a one is of [a race] the source ( A^aSol ) of generosity, or nobleness. (S. [In the PS, mn is here put in the place of fY : but fY is often used in phrases of the same kind and meaning as that above, in the sense of mino .]) IKh cites from Jereer, fiY yuw^obuw^i Almajodi wabuHobuwHi Alkaramo [ Of a race the source of glory, and the very heart of generosity, or nobleness ]: but Aboo-'Alee El- Kálee quotes the words thus; fiY Diy^oDiy^i Almajodi wa buw^obuwo'i Alkaramo [which may be rendered, of a race the source of glory, and the very root of generosity ]; whence it appears that buw^obuw'N is a dial. var. of buw^obuw^N in the sense here given. (TA.) ― -b2- The middle of a thing; (K;) [and app. the heart, or very heart, thereof; the middle as being the best part of a thing;] like buHobuwHN . (TA.) ― -b3- [Hence, perhaps,] The pupil, or apple, or the image that is seen reflected in the black, ( Eayor AA, T, or A_inosaAn K,) of the eye. (AA, T, K.) Whence the saying, huwa A^aEaz~u EalaY~i mino buw^obuw^i EayoniY [ He is dearer to me than the apple of my eye; a saying common in the present day, with the substitution of A_inosaAn for buw^obuw^ ]. (TA.) ― -b4- A generous, or noble, (ISk, T,) or a clever, an ingenious, or an accomplished, or a well-bred, or an elegant, (M, K,) and a light, an active, or a sprightly, (M,) lord, master, chief, or personage: (ISk, T, M, K:) fem. with p . (IKh, TA.) ― -b5- Also, (AA, T, S, * [but I find it only in one of three copies of the S,]) or ↓ buw^obuw^o'N , and ↓ baA^obaA='N , (K,) the last from the M, (TA, [but it is not in the M as transcribed in the TT,]) A learned man (AA, T, S, K) who teaches; (AA, T;) but the teaching of others is not a condition required in the application of the epithet; (TA;) like sarosuwrN . (S [in which this last word is evidently given as a syn.: but in the K it is given to show the form, only, of buw^obuwo'N ].) ― -b6- Also The body of a locust, (K,) without the head and legs. (TA.) ― -b7- And, accord. to the K, The head, or uppermost part, of a vessel in which [the collyrium called ] kuHol is kept: but it will appear, in art. yA^ , that this is [perhaps] a mistranscription for yuw^oyuw^N . (TA.)

definition: [ A sea: and a great river: ] a spacious place comprising a large quantity of water;
sourceDefinition: [ A sea: and a great river: ] a spacious place comprising a large quantity of water; (B;) a large quantity of water, (K, TA,) whether salt or sweet; (TA;) contr. of bar~N ; (S, A;) so called because of its depth (S, TA) and large extent; (S, Msb, TA;) from AlbaHaArapu ; (A;) or because its bed is trenched in the earth; see 1: (TA:) or a large quantity of salt water, only; (K;) and so called because of its saltness: (El-Umawee, TA: [but accord. to the A, this word as an epithet meaning “ salt ” is tropical:]) or rather this is its general meaning: (TA:) for it signifies also any great river; (S, M, TA;) any river of which the water does not cease to flow; (Zj, T, TA;) such as the Euphrates, for instance; (S;) or such as the Tigris, and the Nile, and other similar great rivers of sweet water; of which the great salt baHor is the place of confluence; so called because trenched in the earth: (T, TA:) pl. [of pauc.] A^aboHurN and [of mult.] biHaArN and buHuwrN . (S, Msb, K.) The dim. is ↓ A^ubayoHirN , (K,) which is anomalous; and ↓ buHayorN , which is the regular form: accord. to the K, the latter is not used; but this is untrue; for it is sometimes used, though rare. (MF.) ― -b2- Hence its application in the saying of the Arabs, yaA haAdiYa All~ayoli jurota A_in~amaA huwa AlbaHoru A^awi Alfajoru , which Th explains by saying that the meaning is, (tropical:) [ O guide of the night, thou hast deviated from the right way: ] it is only destruction or thou wilt see the daybreak: the night is here likened to the sea [and with the night is associated the idea of destruction]: but accord. to one recital, it is Albajoru , instead of AlbaHoru . (TA. [See art. bjr .]) ― -b3- Also (tropical:) Salt; as an epithet, applied to water. (S, A.) ― -b4- (tropical:) A fleet, or swift, and excellent, horse; (As, K;) that runs much; (As, TA;) that takes a wide range in his running; (S, A, Msb, B;) that runs like the sea, or a great river; or like the sea, or a great river, when it rolls wave over wave. (Niftaweyh;, TA.) ― -b5- (tropical:) A generous man; (K, TA;) one who takes a wide range in his beneficence, bounty, or kindness; who abounds therein. (TA.) You say, laqiytu bizayodK baHorFA (tropical:) [ I found, in the place of Zeyd, a man of abundant generosity or beneficence ]: b here denoting substitution. (The Lubáb cited in the TA voce bi .) And laqiytu minohu baHorFA (tropical:) [ I found him to be a man of exceeding generosity ]; a phrase expressing an intensive degree of generosity: and raA^ayotu minohu baHorFA [signifies the same]. (Mughnee in art. bi .) ― -b6- (tropical:) A man of extensive knowledge or science; one who takes a wide range in his knowledge or science. (B.) ― -b7- (tropical:) Any person, or thing, that takes a wide range in a thing. (B.) ― -b8- (assumed tropical:) Land of seed-produce and fruitfulness; or a tract, or region, in which are green herbs or leguminous plants, and waters; or the part of a country near to water; syn. riyfN : (Aboo-' Alee, K:) and the dim. ↓ buHayorN is used in the same sense; or, by poetic licence, for ↓ buHayorapN . (TA.) So in the Kur [xxx. 40], Zahara AlfasaAdu fiY Albar~i wa AlbaHori (assumed tropical:) [ Corruption hath appeared in the desert, or deserts, and in the land of seed-produce and fruitfulness; &c.]: (Aboo-'Alee, TA:) or the meaning here is, [ in the desert, or deserts, and in the towns, or villages, in which is water: (see bar~N :) or in the open country and ] in the cities [or towns ] upon the rivers; by sterility in the former, and scarcity in the latter: (Zj, TA, and T in art. br :) or in the land and the sea; i. e., the land has become sterile, or unfruitful, and the supply of the sea has become cut off. (Az, TA.) definition: A wide tract of land: so accord.
sourceDefinition: A wide tract of land: so accord. to Aboo-Nasr: but in one place he says, a small valley in rugged land: pl. biHaArN . (TA.) ― -b2- A land, country, or territory, belonging to, or inhabited by, a people; syn. balodapN . (S, K.) One says, h`*ihi baHoratunaA This is our land, &c.; syn. A^aroDunaA . (S.) It occurs also in the dim. form [↓ buHayorapN ], as in the Towsheeh of El-Jelál. (TA.) ― -b3- Any town, or village, that has a running river and wholesome water: (K:) and [absolutely] any town, or village: of such the Arabs say, h`*ihi baHoratunaA This is our town, or village: and the pl. biHaArN they apply to cities, as well as towns, or villages. (TA.) ― -b4- Low, or depressed, land: (IAar, K:) occurring also in the dim. form [↓ buHayorapN ]. (TA.) ― -b5- A meadow; or a garden; syn. rawoDapN : (T, TA:) or one that is large, (K,) and wide. (TA.) ― -b6- A place where water stagnates. (Sh, K.) ― -b7- The pl. is ↓ baHorN , (as in some copies of the K, [or this is a coll. gen. n. of which baHorapN is the n. un.,]) or biHarN , (as in other copies of the K and in the TA,) or buHorN , (as in the CK,) and biHaArN . sourceDefinition: , a post-classical word, (S, K,) used by the physicians, signifying The crisis of a disease; the sudden change which happens to a sick person, (S, TA,) and the commencement of convalescence, (TA,) in acute diseases; (S, TA;) at a time fixed by some motion in the heavenly bodies, mostly by a motion of the moon; being a change to health or to the contrary: a word [said to be] of Greek origin. definition: A she-camel having her ear slit: (S, * A, Msb, K *:) [and, as a subst.
sourceDefinition: A she-camel having her ear slit: (S, * A, Msb, K *:) [and, as a subst., or an epithet in which the quality of a subst. is predominant,] a she-camel of which the mother was a saAy^ibap ; (Fr, S, Mgh, Msb, K;) i. e., of which the mother had brought forth ten females consecutively before her, and of which the ear was slit; (Mgh;) or of which the mother had brought forth five, of which five the last, if a male, was slaughtered and eaten, but if a female, her ear was slit and she was left with her mother; (Mgh, * Msb;) the predicament of which was the same as that of her mother; (Fr, S, K;) i. e., what was unlawful with respect to her mother was unlawful with respect to herself: (TA:) or a she-camel, or ewe, or she-goat, that had brought forth five young ones, and of which the fifth, if a male, was slaughtered, and its flesh was eaten by the men and women; but if a female, her ear was slit, and it was unlawful to the Arabs to eat her flesh and to drink her milk and to ride her; but when she died, her flesh was lawful to the women: (K:) so says Az, on the authority of Ibn-'Arafeh: (TA: [but it appears from the explanation in the Msb, quoted above, that it was the slit-eared young she-camel here mentioned, not the mother, that was thus termed:]) or a she-camel, or ewe , or she-goat, which, having brought forth ten young ones, had her ear slit, (K,) and no use was made of her milk nor of her back, (TA,) and she was left at liberty to pasture, (K,) and to go to water, (TA,) and her flesh, when she died, was made unlawful to the women of the Arabs, but was eaten by the men: (K:) or one that was left at liberty, without a pastor: (K:) or, as some say, syn. with saAy^ibapN ; i. e., say they, a she-camel which, having brought forth seven young ones, had her ear slit, and was not ridden, nor used for carrying: (Msb:) or a she-camel that had brought forth five young ones, the last of which was a male, in which case her ear was slit, and she was exempted from being ridden and from carrying and from being slaughtered, and not prevented from taking of any water to which she came, nor from any pasturage, nor even ridden by a weary man who, having become unable to proceed in his journey, his means having failed him, or his camel that bore him stopping with him from fatigue or breaking down or perishing, might chance to find her: (Aboo-Is- hák the Grammarian, TA: [and the like, but less fully, is said in the Mgh:]) or, applied specially to a ewe, or she-goat, one that, having brought forth five young ones, had her ear slit: (L, K, TA: [in the CK, for buHirat is put nuHirat :]) it also signifies a she-camel (L) abounding in milk: (L, K:) the pl. is baHaAy^iru and buHurN ; (L, K;) the latter a strange form of pl. of a fem. sing. such as bHyrp ; and said to be the only instance of the kind except SurumN pl. of SariymapN , meaning “ having her ear cut off. ” (TA.) It is said in a trad., that the person who instituted the practices relative to the bHyrp and the HaAmiY , and the first who altered the religion of Ishmael, was 'Amr the son of Loheí the son of Kama'ah the son of Jundab; and these practices are forbidden in the Kur v. 102. (TA.)

definition: , applied to a camel, the male and the female, (S, Mgh, Msb, K,) That has cut its nAb [or tush ];
sourceDefinition: , applied to a camel, the male and the female, (S, Mgh, Msb, K,) That has cut its nAb [or tush ]; (S, Msb, K;) by its entering the ninth year; (Msb;) or in its ninth year; (S, Mgh, K;) for then it cuts that tooth; (S, K;) or, as is sometimes the case, in the eighth year; (S;) and after this there is no age named: (IAar, K:) or a she-camel that has completed her ninth year, and attained her full strength: (Ham p. 506:) and ↓ bazuwlN signifies the same, applied to the male and the female: (IDrd, K:) or, accord. to AZ, a she-camel is not termed baAzilN ; but the epithet ↓ bazuwlN is applied to her that has completed a year after cutting the tooth above mentioned, until she is termed nAb : (MF, TA:) the pl. (of bAzl , S, Msb) is bawaAzilu (S, Msb, K) and buz~alN (S, K) and buzolN , (S,) or buzulN , like kutubN . (K.) baAzilu EaAmK and baAzilu EaAmayoni signify That has passed a year, and two years, after cutting the tooth above mentioned. (MF, TA.) ― -b2- Also The tooth that has come forth at the time above mentioned: (S, K:) pl. bawaAzilu . (IAar, K.) ― -b3- And (tropical:) A man perfect in his experience and his intellect: (K, TA:) or rendered firm, or sound, in judgment by age and experience: so says IDrd: likened to the camel thus termed: (TA:) or old: opposed to ja*aEN , q. v. (IAar in art. j*E of the TA.) ― -b4- And (tropical:) A case, or an affair, and an opinion, firmly settled or established. (TA.) ― -b5- xaTobN baAzilN (assumed tropical:) A difficult, a distressing, or an afflicting, thing, affair, or business. (TA.) You say also, bulaYa biA^a$ohaba baAzilK (assumed tropical:) He was afflicted with a difficult and distressing thing or event. (TA. [See also art. $hb .]) ― -b6- $aj~apN baAzilapN A wound in the head from which the blood flows: (S:) or such as is termed HaAriSapN , (K,) i. e. mutalaAHimapN , (TA,) [but see these two words, and see $aj~apN ,] that cleaves the skin, but does not penetrate beyond it: (K:) the mulet for which is said to be three camels. (TA.) ― -b7- maA baqiyta lahumo baAzilapN is like the saying maA baqiyta lahumo vaAgiyapN wa laA raAgiyapN , i. e. (tropical:) [ There remained not to them ] one [ sheep or goat, or camel ]. (S, TA.) You say also, maA Einodahu baAzilapN , i. e. (assumed tropical:) There is not in his possession anything of property, or of camels &c.: (Yaakoob, S, K:) or, a sufficiency, or a sufficiency of the means of subsistence, that will satisfy a want. (Z, TA.) And laA taraka A@ll~`hu Einodahu baAzilapF (assumed tropical:) [ May God not leave in his possession ] anything. (S.) And lamo yuEoTihimo baAzilapF (assumed tropical:) [ He did not give them ] anything. (S.)

definition: , aor. , (K,) inf. n. baTaAnapN , (TA,) He (a man) was, or became, big, or large, in the belly, (K, TA,) in consequence of much eating. (TA.) ― -b2- And baTina , aor. , inf. n. baTanN , He (a man)...
sourceDefinition: , aor. , (K,) inf. n. baTaAnapN , (TA,) He (a man) was, or became, big, or large, in the belly, (K, TA,) in consequence of much eating. (TA.) ― -b2- And baTina , aor. , inf. n. baTanN , He (a man) was, or became, big, or large, in the belly, in consequence of satiety, (S, TA,) and disordered therein: (TA:) he was, or became, in a state of repletion, or much filled with food. (TA.) ― -b3- ― -b4- And [hence,] baTina signifies also (tropical:) i. q. A^a$ira and baTira [ He exulted, or exulted greatly, or excessively, and behaved insolently and unthankfully, or ungratefully: &c.]. (TA.) ― -b5- buTina He (a man, S, TA) had a complaint of, or a disease in, or a pain in, his belly. (S, Msb, TA.) -A2- baTanahu , (S, K,) aor. , (S, TA,) inf. n. baTonN , (TA,) He struck, or beat, his belly; as also baTana lahu , (S, K,) accord. to some, or the l is added [only] in verse; (S;) and ↓ bT~nhu , (K,) inf. n. taboTiynN . (TA.) ― -b2- It (a disease) entered into him: [as though it penetrated into his belly: see 10:] in this sense it has for its inf. n. buTuwnN . (TA.) And baTanato bihi AlHum~aY The fever produced an effect within him. (TA.) ― -b3- He entered into it; namely, a valley; (S, TA;) in which sense it has for its inf. n. baTonN ; and ↓ tbT~nhu signifies the same: or the latter, he went about in it; namely, the valley; as also ↓ AstbTnhu . (TA.) ― -b4- (tropical:) [ He penetrated into it mentally; ] he knew it; (Msb, K, TA;) namely, the news or story, or the state or case, of another: (K, TA:) (tropical:) he knew the inward, or intrinsic, state or circumstances thereof; (S, Msb, TA;) i. e., of a case, or an affair; (S, TA;) as also ↓ AstbTnhu : (K, A, TA:) and ↓ tbT~nhu (assumed tropical:) he entered into it so that he knew its inward, or intrinsic, state or circumstances. (Ham p. 688.) ― -b5- baTana bifulaAnK , accord. to the S and M, but in the K mino fulaAnK , (TA,) (tropical:) He became one of his particular, or special, intimates, friends, or associates, (S, K, TA,) entering into his affair [or affairs ]: (TA:) or baTana bihi , aor. , inf. n. buTuwnN and baTaAnapN , means (assumed tropical:) he entered into his affair [or affairs ]. (TA.) ― -b6- And baTana , (Msb, K,) aor. , said of a thing, (Msb,) It was, or became, unapparent, hidden, concealed, or covert; (K, TA;) contr. of Zahara . (Msb.) ― -b7- See also 4.

definition: The belly, or abdomen;
sourceDefinition: The belly, or abdomen; i. e. the part of the body which is separated from the jawof [i. e. chest, or thorax, ] by the HijaAb [i. e. midriff, or diaphragm ]; containing the liver and the spleen and the stomach and the lower intestines &c.; (Zj in his “ Khalk el-Insán; ” [in which it is erroneously said to comprise also the lungs;]) contr. of ZahorN ; (S, Msb, K;) of a man and of any animal: (TA:) of the masc. gender, (S, K,) and, accord. to AO, fem. also: (AHát, S:) pl. A^aboTunN and buTuwnN (Az, Msb, K) and buTonaAnN ; (K;) the first a pl. of pauc.; and the second [as also the third] a pl. of mult., applied to more than ten. (Az, TA.) [Hence,] *uw AlbaToni [ What is in the belly: but generally meaning] excrement, ordure, or dung. (K, TA.) You say, A^aloqaY *aA baTonihi He (a man) ejected his excrement, or ordure. (TA.) And A^aloqato *aA baTonihaA She (a woman, TA) brought forth; (K;) as also waDaEato *aAta baTonihaA : (TA in art. *w :) and she (a hen) laid an egg. (K.) And navarato *aA baTonihaA , (T and Mgh in art. nvr ,) and [elliptically] navarato baTonahaA , (T and A and Mgh in that art.,) She (a woman) brought forth many children. (T in that art.) And it is said in a prov., (TA,) Al*~iy^obu yugobaTu bi*iY baTonihi [ The wolf is envied for what is in his belly ]: for one never thinks him to be hungry, but only thinks him to be in a state of repletion, because of his hostility to men and cattle, (A'Obeyd, K,) though he is sometimes distressed by hunger. (A'Obeyd. [See various readings of this prov. in Freytag's Arab. Prov. i. 500 and 501.]) maAtato fiY baTonK , a phrase occurring in a trad., means She (a woman) died in childbirth. (TA.) See also fulaAnN A@bonu baTonihi. baTanN . means (assumed tropical:) Such a one is solicitous for his belly. (Er-Rághib, TA in art. bnY .) [Many phrases in which the word baTon occurs will be found explained under other words of those phrases; as ZahorN , and A^axa*a , and EuSofuwrN , &c.] baTonu AlHuwti : see Alr~i$aA='u . ― -b2- Also The inside, or interior, of anything; syn. jawofN : and so ↓ baATinN ; syn. daAxilN : (K:) pl. of the former as above. (TA.) Thus baTonu waAdK means The interior of a water-course or riverbed [or valley; i. e. its bottom, in which flows, occasionally or constantly, its torrent or river ]. (MA.) And baTonu mak~apa means The interior of Mekkeh. (Bd in xlviii. 24.) [Hence,] it is said of the Kur-án, likul~i A=yapK minohaA ZahorN wa baTonN , meaning (assumed tropical:) To every verse thereof is an apparent sense and a sense requiring development. (TA.) [See ZahorN .] See also baATinN . [And its pl. buTonaAnN is also used as a sing., meaning The middle, or midst, of a thing: and the lower, or lowest, part, or the foundation. Thus,] buTonaAnu Aljan~api means The middle, or midst, of Paradise: (S, TA:) and buTonaAnu AlEaro$i , The lower, or lowest, part, or the foundation, of the Er$ [vulgarly held to be the throne of God ]. (TA.) You say also [ baTonu Alkaf~i and] Alkaf~i ↓ baATinu (assumed tropical:) The palm of the hand [opposed to ZahoruhaA and ZaAhiruhaA ]: and [ baTonu Alqadami and] Alqadami ↓ baATinu (assumed tropical:) The sole of the foot [likewise opposed to ZahoruhaA and ZaAhiruhaA ]: (Zj in his “ Khalk- el-Insán: ”) and baTonu AlHaAfiru (S in art. nsr ) and AlHaAfiri ↓ baATinu (M and K in that art.) (assumed tropical:) [ The sole of the solid hoof; ] the part of the solid hoof in which is the nasor , q. v. (S and M and K in that art.) baTonu Alr~aAHapi is well known [as another name for baTonu Alkaf~i , explained above; for Alr~aAHap is often used as syn. with Alkaf~ ]: and Alxuf~i ↓ baATinu is [said to be] (assumed tropical:) The part of the foot of a camel or the like that is next the leg: and one says, ↓ baATinu AlA_iboTi , [meaning (assumed tropical:) The armpit, or hollow of the inner side of the shoulder-joint, ] but not baTonu AlA_iboTi : (TA:) [and AlEunuqi ↓ baATinu the throat. ] The baTon of a feather is (tropical:) The long, (S,) or longer, (K,) [or wider, i. e. inner, ] lateral half: pl. buTonaAnN ; (S, K, TA;) which is explained as signifying the parts beneath the shaft: opposed to ZuhoraAnN , pl. of ZahorN [q. v.]. (TA.) ― -b3- Also A low, or depressed, tract, or portion, of land, or ground; (S, TA;) and so ↓ baATinN : (TA:) [or a bottom, or low land; or a low, soft flat; i. e.] soft, plain, fine, low land or ground; opposed to ZahorN [q. v.]: (TA in art. Zhr :) pl. of the former, (S,) or of the latter, (K,) buTonaAnN , (S, K,) a pl. of mult., (TA,) and A^aboTinapN , (K,) a pl. of pauc., and anomalous [as pl. of either]: (TA:) the former pl., in relation to land, is also used as a sing., like baTonN : (AHn, TA:) and accord. to ISh, buTonaAnu AlA^aroDi signifies the low, or depressed, tract, or tracts, of land, of the plain, or soft, parts thereof, and of the rugged, and of the meadows, where water rests and stagnates: and such tracts are also called bawaATinu and buTuwnN . (TA.) ― -b4- baTonu Als~amaA='i and Zahoru Als~amaA='i both signify (assumed tropical:) The apparent, visible, part of the sky. (Fr, T voce ZahorN [q. v.].) -A2- Also (tropical:) A tribe below that which is termed qabiylap : (S, Msb, K, TA:) or next below the EimaArap : (S and TA voce $aEobN , &c.:) or below the faxi* and above the EmArp : (K: [but for this I have found no other authority:]) of the masc. gender: (TA:) or [properly] fem.: but if Hay~N [said by some to signify a tribe, absolutely,] be meant thereby, it is masc.: (Msb:) or fem. if used in the sense of qabiylap : (TA:) pl. [of pauc.] A^aboTunN and [of mult.] buTuwnN . (Msb, K.) [See $aEobN .]

definition: One of the Mansions of the Moon;
sourceDefinition: One of the Mansions of the Moon; (S, K;) namely, the Second; (Kzw, &c.;) three small stars [e and p and n], (S, K,) disposed in the form of an equilateral triangle, (S,) as though they were three stones whereon a cooking-pot is placed, and forming the belly of the Ram; (S, K;) the appellation being made a diminutive because the Ram consists of many stars in the form of a ram; [so I here render Hamal though it properly signifies a lamb;] the $azaTaAni being its two horns; and the buTayon , its belly; [or, accord. to our configuration of Aries, the rump;] and the vuray~aA , its rump, or tail; (S;) three obscure stars, forming the points of a triangle, in the belly of the Ram, between the $araTaAni and the vuray~aA ; (Kzw, Mir-át ez-Zemán, &c.;) the three stars of which two are on the tail and one on the thigh of the Ram, forming an equilateral triangle. (Kzw in his description of Aries.) [See manaAzilu Alqamari , in art. nzl .] The Arabs assert that it has no nawo' [here meaning effect upon the weather], except wind. (TA.)

definition: The lining, or inner covering, of a garment, or piece of cloth [&c.
sourceDefinition: The lining, or inner covering, of a garment, or piece of cloth [&c.]; contr. of ZihaArapN ; (S, Msb, K;) as also ↓ baATinapN : (JK in art. Zhr :) pl. of the former baTaAy^nu . (TA.) ― -b2- (assumed tropical:) A secret (K, TA) that a man conceals. (TA.) One says, huwa *uw biTaAnapK bifulaAnK , i. e. (assumed tropical:) He is one who possesses knowledge of the inward, or intrinsic, state or circumstances of the case, or affair, of such a one. (TA.) ― -b3- (tropical:) A particular, or special, intimate, friend, or associate; (S, K, TA;) one who is particularly distinguished by entering into, and becoming acquainted with, the inward, or intrinsic, state or circumstances of one's case or affair; (TA;) an intimate and familiar friend or associate; (Zj, TA;) a confidential friend, who is consulted respecting one's circumstances: (TA:) it is from the same word in the sense first explained above, relating to a garment, or piece of cloth: (Mgh, Er-Rághib:) and is used in a pl. sense, as meaning intimate and familiar friends or associates, to whom one is open, or unreserved, in conversation, and who know the inward state or circumstances [ of one's case or affair ]: (Zj, TA:) or one's family; and one's particular, or special, intimates, friends, or associates. (Mgh.) You say, huwa biTaAnatiY (tropical:) [ He is my particular, or special, intimate, &c.]: and humo biTaAnatiY and A^aholu biTaAnatiY (tropical:) [ They are my particular, or special, intimates, &c.]. (A, TA.) See also 4. ― -b4- Coupled with EalaAwap , it signifies What is put beneath [ the things that compose the main load of a camel ], such as a water-skin and the like. (TA.) ― -b5- See also baATinapN .

definition: is a particle; (S, Msb, Mughnee;) contr. of laA : (S:) not a noun: (Sb, S:) it is a replicative; (S, Mughnee;) an affirmative of what is said [in that to which it is a reply]; (S, Msb;) [with very...
sourceDefinition: is a particle; (S, Msb, Mughnee;) contr. of laA : (S:) not a noun: (Sb, S:) it is a replicative; (S, Mughnee;) an affirmative of what is said [in that to which it is a reply]; (S, Msb;) [with very few exceptions] relating only to a negation, which it annuls: (Msb, Mughnee:) the final letter is a radical: or, accord. to some, the word is originally balo , [after which an affirmation is to be understood,] and the final letter is augmentative: and some of these say that this letter is a denotative of the fem. gender, because it is [often] pronounced with imáleh. (Mughnee.) It is a reply to an interrogation in which is a negative, (T, M, Msb, Mughnee, K,) and affirms what is said to thee [in that interrogation]; (M, K;) whether it be an interrogation in the proper sense, (Mughnee,) as when you say to another, A^alamo tafoEalo ka*aA [ Didst thou not such a thing? ], and he replies, balaY [meaning Yes, or yea, or ay, I did], (T,) or as when one says, A^alayosa zayodN biqaAy^imK [ Is not Zeyd standing? ], and you reply, balaY [ Yes, he is]; or be meant to convey reproof, (Mughnee,) as in the Kur [lxxv. 3 and 4], A^ayaHosabu AlA_inosaAnu A^ano lano najomaEa EiZaAmahu balaY [ Doth man think that we will not collect his bones? (S, TA.) AHn speaks of a kind of plank as being used fiY binaA='i Als~ufuni [ in the construction of ships ]: but binaA='N is originally used only in relation to that which does not grow; as stone, and clay, and the like. definition: He made him to build, frame, or construct, a house, or tent: (S:) or he gave him a building: or he gave him that wherewith to build a house: (M, K:) and AbnAhu bayotFA he gave him a house, or tent, to build or frame or construct.
sourceDefinition: He made him to build, frame, or construct, a house, or tent: (S:) or he gave him a building: or he gave him that wherewith to build a house: (M, K:) and AbnAhu bayotFA he gave him a house, or tent, to build or frame or construct. (T.) It is said in a prov., AlmiEozay tubohiY walaA tuboniY [ Goats rend, or make holes, and render vacant, and do not afford materials for fabricating tents ]; i. e., they do not yield hair of which a tent is fabricated; (T, S; *) for the tents of the Arabs [of the desert] are of the kind called TiraAf , made of skin, and A^axobiyap , made of wool or of camels' fur, and not of $aEar [by which is especially meant goats' hair], (S,) or, as is found in the handwriting of Aboo-Sahl, of wool or of skin: (TA:) or the meaning is, goats rend tents, or pierce them with holes, by their leaping upon them, (T and S in art. bhw ,) so that they cannot be inhabited, (S in that art.,) and do not aid in the fabrication of tents; for the goats of the Arabs of the desert have short hair, not long enough to be spun; whereas the goats of the cold countries, and of the people of the fertile regions, have abundant hair, and of this the Akrád [or Kurdees] fabricate their tents. (T.) ― -b2- [Hence,] He introduced him to his wife [ on the occasion of his marriage ]: whence the saying of 'Alee, mataY tubonyiniY , accord. to IAth properly meaning mataY tajoEaluniY A^aboniY bizawojatiY [ When wilt thou make me to have my wife conducted to me? or, to go in to my wife? ]. (TA.)

definition: [originally an inf.
sourceDefinition: [originally an inf. n.: (see 1, first sentence:) then applied to A building; a structure; an edifice; ] a thing that is built, or constructed; pl. A^aboniyapN , and pl. pl. A^aboniyaAtN : (M, K:) and ↓ bunoyaAnN [also] has this meaning; (Msb;) [and is likewise originally an inf. n.;] or this signifies a wall; syn. HaAy^iTN ; (S;) or it may be a pl., [or rather a coll. gen. n., meaning buildings, structures, edifices, or walls, ] of which the sing. [or n. un.] is ↓ bunoyaAnapN , and as such may be masc. and fem: (Er-Rághib, TA:) ↓ binoyapN and ↓ bunoyapN also signify [the same as binaA='N as explained above; or] a thing that one has built, framed, or constructed; (M, K;) or, accord. to some, the former of these two relates to objects of the senses, and the latter to objects of the mind, to glory or honour or the like; (MF, TA;) and their pls. are ↓ binFY and ↓ bunFY ; (K;) or, accord. to the S and M, these two appear to be sings.; (TA;) [or they may be pls. or sings.; for J says that] AlbunaY is like AlbinaY ; one says, bunoyapN and bunFY , and binoyapN and binFY ; (S;) [and ISd says that] binoyapN and bunoyapN signify as above, and so binFY and bunFY ; or, accord. to Aboo-Is-hák, binFY is pl. of binoyapN ; or it may be used by poetic licence for binaA='N : (M:) accord. to IAar, binFY signifies buildings, or structures, of clay: and also [ tents ] of wool; (T;) and binaA='N likewise signifies a tent (M, TA) in which the Arabs of the desert dwell, in the desert, (TA,) such as is called xibaA=' ; (M, TA; *) and TiraAfN and qub~apN and miDorabN are names applied to dwellings of the same kind; (TA;) pl. A^aboniyapN : (M:) the moveable dwelling, such as the xayomap and miZal~ap and fusoTaAT and suraAdiq and the like, is called binaA='N as being likened to the building of burnt bricks and of clay and of gypsum. (M.) [See also baniy~apN .] ― -b2- Also The roof, or ceiling, of a house or chamber or the like; as in the Kur [ii. 20], Al~a*iY jaEala lakumu AlA^aroDa firA$FA wa Als~amaA='a binaA='F [ Who hath made for you the earth as a bed, and the heaven as a roof, or ceiling ]: (S, [but wanting in some copies,] and Jel:) so says AZ: (S:) or the meaning here is, as a tent ( qub~ap ) pitched over you. (Bd.) ― -b3- And The body, with the limbs or members. (TA.) ― -b4- And i. q. niToEN [ A thing that is spread on the ground to serve as a table for food &c., made of leather; like mibonaApN ]: occurring in a trad., where it is mentioned as spread on the ground, on a day of rain, for Mohammad to pray upon: so says Sh. (T.)

The Kaabeh is also called baniy~apu A_iboraAhiyma [ The building of Abraham ]; because he built it. (TA.)

definition: [ Building, framing, or constructing ]: accord.
sourceDefinition: [ Building, framing, or constructing ]: accord. to A'Obeyd, its pl. is A^abonaA='N ; and in like manner, A^ajonaA='N is pl. of jaAnK : and hence the prov., A^abonaAw^uhaA A^ajonaAw^uhaA , (M,) or A^ajonaAw^uhaA A^abonaAw^uhaA , i. e. The injurers thereof, meaning this house ( h`*ihi Ald~aAr ), by demolishing it, are the builders thereof. (S in art. jnY .) ISd says, I am of opinion that these two pls. are not used except in this prov.: and J says, in art. jnY , I think that the prov. is originally junaAtuhaA bunaAtuhaA ; but IB affirms that it is not so: and he says that the prov. is applied to him who does, or makes, a thing without consideration, and commits a fault therein, which he repairs by undoing what he has done or made: it originated from the fact that the daughter of a certain king of El-Yemen, during his absence on a military expedition, built, by the advice of others, a house, which he, disliking it, commanded them to demolish. (TA in art. jnY . [See also Freytag's Arab. Prov. i. 294.]) ― -b2- A bridegroom: from banaY EalaY A^aholihi [q. v.]. (TA.) And hence, Any one going in to his wife. (S, TA.) ― -b3- qawosN baAniypN A bow cleaving to its string (T, S, M, K) so that it (the latter) almost breaks; (T, S, M;) the doing of which is a fault; (M;) contr. of baAy^inapN [q. v.]: (S and M in art. byn :) and so ↓ baAnaApN (T, M, K) in the dial. of Teiyi: (T, M:) or the latter signifies widely separate from its string [like baAy^inapN ]. (TA.)

(M, K.) One says, [likening a man to a camel lying down,] A^aloqaY bawaAniyhu , meaning He took up his abode, and settled, (T, M, K,) in a place; like A^aloqaY EaSaAhu . (T, M.) A^aloqaY Al$~aA^omu bawaAniyahu [meaning Syria became in a settled state ] occurs in a trad. as related by A'Obeyd: and if he said bawaAy^inahu , it would be allowable; bawaAy^inu being pl. of bwAn , [i. e. buwaAnN or biwaAnN ,] which is a name for any tent-pole except in the middle of the bayot , which has three poles. (T.) And it is said in another trad., A^aloqati Als~amaA='u biraka bawaAniyhaA , meaning The sky cast down the rain that it contained. (TA.)

The fem. of AibonN is ↓ AibonapN or A@bonapN [with the conjunctive A when not commencing a sentence] and ↓ binotN [meaning A daughter; and (assumed tropical:) any female descendant ]: (T, S, M, Mgh, Msb, K:) accord. to Sb, (M,) AibonapN is formed from AibonN by affixing h [or p ]; but not so binotN ; for this is formed by affixing Y as a letter of quasi-coordination, and then substituting for it t : (M, K:) [but if the t be substituted for Y , it seems more probable that the Y is the final radical:] or, as some say, the t is substituted for w : (M:) [Mtr says,] the t is substituted for the final radical: (Mgh:) accord. to Ks, it is originally with h [or p ], because it has a fem. meaning: (IAar, Msb:) [my own opinion is most agreeable with this of Ks; and with that of Zj, which will be mentioned below; or, perhaps, is identical with that of Zj: I think it most probable that, as AibonN is generally held to be originally banaYN or banawN , so AibonapN and binotN are both originally banayapN or banawapN , and that binotN is formed from AibonapN by suppressing the alif, transferring its kesreh to the b , making the n quiescent, and changing the p into t , which is therefore said to be not the sign of the fem. gender, either because it is not p , but is a substitute for p , or because it is preceded by a quiescent letter:] AHn says that the t is substituted for the final radical letter, which is w ; and that it is not the sign of the fem. gender, because the letter [next] before it is quiescent: this [he says] is the opinion of Sb, and is the right opinion; for he says that if you were to use it as the proper name of a man, you would make it perfectly decl.; and if the t were to denote the fem. gender, the name would not be perfectly decl.: (TA:) and the same is said respecting the t in A^uxotN : (TA in art. Axw :) this t remains in a case of pause (Ks, IAar, S, Msb) as in the case of the connexion of the word with a word following: (S:) but one should not say AibinotN , (Th, T, S.) because the A is required only on account of the quiescence of the b , and is therefore dropped when this is made movent: (S:) Zj says that, in forming the pl. of binotN [and of AibonapN ], the sing. is reduced to its original form, which is faEolapN [as I find it written in the transcript from the T in the TT, but it may be a mistake for faEalaPN ,] with the last radical letter suppressed: (T in TT:) the pl. is banaAtN (T, S, Msb) alone: (S:) [and this is generally treated as a fem. pl. of the perfect, or sound, kind, although the t in binotN is said to be not a sign of the fem. gender; so that you say, raA^ayotu banaAtika I saw thy daughters; but sometimes] one says, raA^ayotu banaAtaka , with fet-h [as the case-ending], treating the t as a radical letter. (S.) It is said in the Bári' that when men and women are mixed together, the masc. pl. is made predominant; so that one says, banuw fulaAnK [meaning The sons and daughters, or the children, of such a one ]; and even, AimoraA^apN mino banY tamiymK [ A woman of the children of Temeem ]; and accordingly, if banuw fulaAnK is applied to denote the persons to whom a legacy is left, the males and the females are included therein. (IAmb, Msb.) ― -b3- ↓ banaAtN also signifies (tropical:) Dolls with which young girls play: (S, Mgh, K:) sing. binotN . (Mgh.) It occurs in this sense in a trad., in which 'Áïsheh speaks of her playing therewith (S, Mgh) when, being nine years of age, she was conducted as a bride to Mohammad. (Mgh.) ― -b4- Aibon is often prefixed to some other noun (T, M, Msb) that particularizes its signification, because of a close connexion between the two meanings: (Msb:) and so is ↓ binot . (T, M.) definition: , of the same measure as A^uEayomK , is the dim.
sourceDefinition: , of the same measure as A^uEayomK , is the dim. of A^abonaY , which is like A^aEomaY , (Sb, IB, Mgh,) and is quasi-pl. of AibonN . (Mgh.) Mohammad is related, in a trad., to have said, A^ubayoniY laA taromuwA jamorapa AlEabaqabipi Hat~aY taToluEa Al$~amosu [ O little (meaning dear ) sons, cast not ye the pebble of the 'Akabeh (see jamorapN ) until the sun rise ], (TA,) or A^ubayoniY~a Alx [ O my little sons &c.]: (Mgh, TA:) IAth says that the hemzeh is augmentative; and that there are differences of opinion respecting the form of the word and its meaning: some say that it is the dim. of A^abonaY , like A^aEomaY , a sing. word denoting a pl. meaning, or, accord. to some, a pl. of AibonN , as well as A^abonaA='N : some say that it is the dim. of AibonN ; [and if so, we must read A^ubayoniY my little son; ] but this requires consideration [more especially as it is followed by a pl. verb]: AO says that it is the dim. of baniY~a , pl. of AibonN with the affixed pronoun of the first pers. [sing.]; and this requires us to read A^ubayoniY~a . (TA.) J says, in the S, that the dim. of A^abonaA='N [pl. of AibonN ] is ↓ A^ubayonaA='N , and, if you will, ↓ A^ubayonuwna ; and he cites a verse in which occurs the expression A^ubayoniyka , [in the gen. case, meaning thy little sons, ] and adds, it is as though its sing. were A_ibonN , with the disjunctive A , whence the dim. ↓ A^ubayonN , in the pl. A^ubayonuwna : but he should have said, as though its sing. were A^abonaY , like A^aEomaY , originally A^abonawu . (IB, TA.)

definition: (T, S, M, K) and mabonaApN (M, K) A niToE [like binaA='N , which see for an explanation]: (S, M, K:) and a sitor [i.
sourceDefinition: (T, S, M, K) and mabonaApN (M, K) A niToE [like binaA='N , which see for an explanation]: (S, M, K:) and a sitor [i. e. curtain or the like ]: (K:) or a thing in the form of a sitor : (M:) or a [ tent of the kind called ] qub~ap , made of skins, or hides: (IAar, T:) or a thing of skins, or hides, of like form to the qub~ap , which a woman places in, or at, the side of her tent ( fiY kisori bayotihaA ), and in which she dwells; and may-be she has sheep, or goats, and is content with the possession of these, exclusively of the other sheep, or goats, for herself and her garments [and app. for making of their skins her mbnAh ]; and she has a covering ( A_izaAr ) [extended] in the middle of the bayot [or tent], within, to protect her from the heat, and from the violent rain, so that she and her clothes are not wetted: (Aboo-'Adnán, T:) or, accord. to As, a mat ( HaSiyrN ), or a niToE , which the trafficker spreads upon the things that he sells: and they used to put the mats ( AlHuSur ) upon the A^anoTaAE [pl. of niToE ], and go round about with them [in the market]: the mbnAp is thus called because it is made of skins joined together: (T:) also a receptacle of the kind called Eayobap : (M, K:) such is said to be its meaning: (S:) pl. mabaAnK . (T.)

sourceDefinition: , (S,) inf. n. talotalapN , (M, K,) He moved him, agitated him, shook him, put him into a state of motion or commotion; (S, M, K;) or did so vehemently: (S, K, and Mgh in art. tr :) he shook him, or shook him violently, (namely, a drinker,) and ordered him to breathe in his face, that he might know whether he had drunk [ wine or the like ], or not; (TA in this art. and art. tr ;) as also tarotarahu , and mazomazahu . (TA in the latter art.) ― -b2- talotalapN also signifies Hard journeying: and rough, or severe, or vehement, driving. (K.) You say, talotala Alr~ajulu The man was rough, or severe, or vehement, in his driving. (M.) -A2- talotalapu bahoraA='a is [The tribe of] Bahrà's pronouncing the t of tafoEaluwna with kesr; (M, K;) saying tifoEaluwna , and ti$ohaduwna , and the like. (M.)

sourceDefinition: , accord. to Lth, [and accord. to general present usage,] A mound, or hill, of dust, or earth, [or rubbish, ] pressed together, not natural: but this is a mistake [if meant as an explanation of the proper application], for with the Arabs it signifies a natural hill: En-Nadr says that it is of the smaller sort of A_ikaAm [pl. of A^akamapN ]; it is of the height of a house, or tent, and the breadth of its back is about ten cubits; it is smaller than the A^akamap , has fewer stones, gives growth to nothing good, and its stones are compacted together exactly like those of the A^akamap : (T:) [the mound, or artificial hill, above mentioned, is what is meant by its being said,] the tal~ of dust, or earth, is well known: and the word signifies also a heap of sand: (M, K:*) in both of these senses from Alt~al~u signifying “ the throwing upon the ground ” anything of a corporeal kind: (M:) also a hill (M, K, TA) overtopping what is adjacent to it: (TA:) pl. [of pauc.] A^atolaAlN (M, TA) and A^atul~N (TA) and [of mult.] tilaAlN (T, S, Msb, K) and tuluwlN . (TA.) -A2- Also A pillow: pl. A^atolaAlN , which is extr.: or the pl. signifies certain sorts of cloths, or of garments: (K, TA:) or, as some say, of pillows. (TA.)

definition: A mode, or manner, of lying upon the side.
sourceDefinition: A mode, or manner, of lying upon the side. (Fr, K.) ― -b2- Sluggishness, laziness, or indolence. (Fr, T, K.) ― -b3- A state, or condition. (S, M, K) You say, huwa bitil~api sawo'K He is in an evil state or condition; like as you say bibiyoy^api sw' : (S:) and baAta bitil~api sawo'K He passed the night in an evil state or condition. (M.) ― -b4- A thing; as in the saying, tal~ahu bitil~api sawo'K [explained above]: see 1. (Th, M, K.) -A2- I. q. bil~apN , (T, M,) or balalN , as also ↓ talalN : (K:) Abu-s-Semeyda' says that til~apN and bil~apN and talalN and tal~apN are all one [i. e. Moisture ]. (T.) One says, [app. to a person suspected of having drunk wine or the like,] maA h`*ihi Alt~il~apu bifiyka i. e. Albal~apu [ What is this moisture in thy mouth? ]. (T, M.)

definition: The waEil [or mountain-goat ], (M, K,) as a general term: (M:) [in the present day, but vulgarly pronounced tayotal , applied to the wild goat of the Arabian and Egyptian deserts and mountains;
sourceDefinition: The waEil [or mountain-goat ], (M, K,) as a general term: (M:) [in the present day, but vulgarly pronounced tayotal , applied to the wild goat of the Arabian and Egyptian deserts and mountains; the capra jaela of Hamilton Smith; called by some an ibex; as is also badan :] or an old wEl : (S, M, Mgh, K:) or the male of the A^arowaY : (Sh, T, M, K: [this is the same as the first explanation:]) En-Nadr says that it has small horns: (T:) Aboo-Kheyreh, that it is of the wuEuwl , does not quit the mountain, and its horns have branches: (T, Mgh: *) he says that the wEwl are dusky, or dingy, or of a hue inclining to black and dust-colour, with whiteness in their lower parts; and the vayaAtil [pl. of vayotal ] are like them in their colours, and only distinguished from them by the horns; the wEl having long horns, which extend backwards until they meet over his tail: (T:) also a species of [ the bovine antelope called ] baqaru AlwaHo$i , (M, K,) that abides in the mountains. (M.) ― -b2- A man who sits with women. (TA.) ― -b3- Incapable of going in to women; or not desirous of women. (K.) ― -b4- A bulky, or corpulent, man, in whom one thinks there is good (AA, K, TA) when there is no good in him: (AA, TA:) but, as mentioned by As, it is tytl . (TA.)

definition: , in its primary sense, is The removing of the varob , i.
sourceDefinition: , in its primary sense, is The removing of the varob , i. e., the fat that forms the integument of the stomach of a ruminant: so says Z. (Har p. 197.) ― -b2- And hence, (tropical:) The act of blaming; reproving; and punishing, or chastising, for an offence, or a crime: (Har ubi suprà:) or (tropical:) severe blaming or reproving, that rends reputations, and takes away the brightness of countenances: (Z in Har ubi suprá:) which last meaning it has in the Kur xii. 92: (Bd:) or laA tavoriyba Ealayokumo there means (assumed tropical:) No evil, or mischief, shall come upon you: (Zj, T:) or (assumed tropical:) your offences, or crimes, shall not be mentioned: (Th, M:) tvryb signifies (assumed tropical:) the act of blaming, or reproving; (S, Mgh;) or doing so severely, or angrily; or, with the utmost severity or harshness: the act of upbraiding, or reproaching: and the going to the utmost length in blaming or reproving: one says, laA tavoriyba Ealayoka (assumed tropical:) [ No blame, &c., shall be laid on thee ]: and it is from Alv~arobu [as explained above]. (S.) You say, vr~b and ↓ varaba and ↓ Avrb , meaning (assumed tropical:) He blamed, or reproved; or did so severely, or with the utmost severity; or reproached, or upbraided: (T:) and vr~b Ealayohi , (S, M, K,) and v~rbhu ; (A, K;) and ↓ varabahu , [and varaba Elyh ,] aor. , (K,) inf. n. varobN ; (TK;) and ↓ Avrbhu ; (A, K;) (assumed tropical:) he blamed him, or reproved him; upbraided him, or reproached him, (M, A, K,) with, or for, his offence, or crime; (M, K;) and reminded him thereof; (M;) he showed him his deed to be foul, abominable, or bad: (As, S:) or Elyh ↓ varaba , aor. , signifies (assumed tropical:) he blamed him, or reproved him; and, as Suh says, vr~b Elyh , (assumed tropical:) he blamed him, or reproved him, much. (Msb.) ― -b3- Also (assumed tropical:) The acting ill, or corruptly; doing evil, or mischief; creating confusion, or disorder. (TA.) -A2- It is also said in the K to be syn. with TaY~N , which means The building [or casing a well] with stones: but [SM says,] I fear that this is a mistranscription for tavowiybN , with w . (TA.)

definition: A thin integument of fat that covers the stomach of a ruminant and the bowels or intestines;
sourceDefinition: A thin integument of fat that covers the stomach of a ruminant and the bowels or intestines; (Lth, T, S, M, Msb, K;) the fat that is spread over the bowels, or intestines: (T:) pl. (of mult., TA) vuruwbN (M, K) and (of pauc., TA) A^avorubN , and pl. pl. A^avaAribu . (K.) Hence, SaArati Al$~amosu kaA@loA^avaAribi The sun [upon the ground] became like the integuments above-mentioned: i. e., scattered; being upon one place and not upon another, towards sunset: a phrase occurring in a trad., in which it is said that when this is the case, it is forbidden to perform the afternoonprayer: and in another trad. occurs the phrase, SaArati Al$~amosu kavarobi Aln~aAqapi [ The sun upon the ground became like the vrb of the she-camel ]. (TA.) ― -b2- And [hence,] (assumed tropical:) A land of which the stones are such as those of the Har~ap [q. v.], save that they are white. (L.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. , inf. n. viqalN (S, Msb, K, &c.) and viqolN , a contraction of the former, (Msb,) and vaqaAlapN , (K, TA, in the CK viqAlap , but) like karaAmapN , (TA,) It (a thing, S, Msb) was, or became, heavy, weighty, or ponderous. (S, K.) [See viqalN , below.] ― -b2- See also 4. ― -b3- [(assumed tropical:) It was, or became, heavy, weighty, or preponderant, ideally. ] faA^am~aA mano vaqulato mawaAziynuhu , in the Kur ci. 5, means (assumed tropical:) And as to him whose good deeds shall be preponderant. (Bd, Jel.) [See also Kur vii. 7 and xxiii. 104.] ― -b4- [(assumed tropical:) It was, or became, heavy, or weighty, as meaning onerous, burdensome, oppressive, afflictive, grievous, or troublesome. ] You say, vaqula Alqawolu (tropical:) The saying was [ heavy, or weighty, &c.; or] unpleasant to be heard. (TA.) And it is said in the Kur vii. 186, vaqulato fiY Als~am`waAti waAlA^aroDi (assumed tropical:) It (the time of the resurrection) will be momentous, or formidable, [ in the heavens and on the earth, or] to the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, (Bd, Jel,) to the angels and men and genii; app. alluding to the wisdom shown in concealing it: (Bd:) or it means the knowledge thereof [ is difficult ]: (Ibn-'Arafeh, TA:) or it is occult, or hidden. (Kt, TA.) [ vaqula is also said of a word, and of a sound, meaning (assumed tropical:) It was heavy, or not easy, of utterance; or heavy to the ear: see 2. And of an affair, or action, meaning (assumed tropical:) It was afflictive, grievous, troublesome, or difficult. In these and similar senses, it is trans. by means of EalaY : you say, vaqula Ealayohi (assumed tropical:) It was, or became, heavy, weighty, onerous, &c., to him. In like manner also it is said of food, meaning (assumed tropical:) It was, or became, heavy to the stomach; difficult of digestion. ] You say also, vaqula samoEuhu (tropical:) [ His hearing was, or became, heavy; or] his hearing partially went. (K, TA.) ― -b5- (tropical:) He (a man) was, or became, heavy in sickness, or disease: [and in like manner, in his sleep:] the verb is thus, with damm to the q ; though said in the K to be vaqila , like fariHa , as meaning his disease became violent; (Fet-h el-Báree, TA;) not improbably through error or inadvertence. (MF.) ― -b6- [(assumed tropical:) He was, or became, heavy, slow, sluggish, indolent, lazy, dull, torpid, or drowsy; wanting in alacrity, activity, agility, animation, spirit, or intelligence; stupid. ] You say, yavoqulu Eano qubuwli maA yuloqaY A_ilayohi (assumed tropical:) [ He is averse from receiving, or accepting, or admitting, or is slow to receive, &c., what is said to him ]. (TA.) ― -b7- Also, said of the Earofaj , and of the vumaAm , (tropical:) Its shoots became luxuriant, or succulent, or sappy. (K, TA.) -A2- vaqalahu , (JK, S, K,) biyadihi , (K,) aor. , (TA,) inf. n. vaqolN , (K,) He tried the weight of it, (JK, S, K,) namely, a thing, (K,) or a sheep or goat, (S,) by lifting it [ with his hand ] to see if it were heavy or light. (S, TA.) ― -b2- vaqala Al$~aYo'u Al$~aYo'a fiY Alwazoni , aor. and inf. n. as above, (S,) The thing surpassed the thing in weight; outweighed it. (PS.) ― -b3- See also 2.

sourceDefinition: , inf. n. tavoqiylN , He, or it, made it, or him, vaqiyl [i. e. heavy, properly and tropically]: (K:) tvqyl is the contr. of taxofiyfN ; (S;) and signifies the making heavy in weight [&c.]; as also vaqolN [inf. n. of ↓ vaqalahu ]. (KL.) ― -b2- [Hence, (assumed tropical:) He made it (a word or a sound) heavy, or not easy, of utterance; or heavy to the ear: and particularly a word by uttering hemzeh with its true, or proper, sound, which is commonly termed taHoqiyqu Alhamozapi , and opposed to taxofiyfuhaA ; and by making a single consonant double; and by making a quiescent consonant movent: often occurring in these senses in lexicons and grammars: opposed to xaf~afahu .]

sourceDefinition: Weight: or a weight: syn. wazonN : (S, Msb, KL:) pl. A^avoqaAlN . (S.) So in the phrase A^aEoTihi viqolahu [ Give thou him his, or its, weight ]. (S, Msb.) See also mivoqaAlN . You say also, A^aloqaY Ealayohi viqolahu or ↓ viqalahu [ He threw upon him his weight: see mivoqaAlN , last sentence: and see jiromN ]. (S in art. Awq &c., accord. to different copies.) ― -b2- And A load, or burden: (KL:) or a heavy load or burden: pl. as above. (K.) wataHomilu A^avoqaAlakumo , in the Kur xvi. 7, means And they carry your loads, or burdens; (Bd;) or your heavy loads or burdens. (TA.) ― -b3- A^avoqaAlN (as pl. of viqolN , K, or of ↓ vaqalN , Bd) also signifies (tropical:) The treasures, or buried treasures, of the earth: and its dead, or corpses. (K, TA, and Bd and Jel in xcix. 2.) ― -b4- Also (as pl. of viqolN , K) (tropical:) Sins. (JK, K.) So in the saying in the Kur [xxix. 12], walayaHomilun~a A^avoqaAlahumo waA^avoqaAlFA maEa A^avoqaAlihimo (tropical:) [ And they shall assuredly bear their sins, and sins (of others whom they have seduced) with their sins ]. (TA.)

definition: A thing, or things, that a man has with him, of such things as burden him: (Ham p.
sourceDefinition: A thing, or things, that a man has with him, of such things as burden him: (Ham p. 295:) [and particularly] the household-goods, or furniture and utensils, (El-Fárábee, JK, S, Mgh, Msb, K, Ham ubi suprà, and Bd in xcix. 2,) and (accord. to El-Fárábee, Msb) the household and kindred and party, or domestics, or servants, (JK, S, Mgh, Msb, K, and Ham,) of a man, (Ham,) or of a traveller: (JK, S, Mgh, Msb, K:) [or the travelling-apparatus and baggage and train, of a man:] pl. A^avoqaAlN ; (JK, S, Mgh, Msb, K; *) with which ↓ vaqilapN is syn., (JK, S, K,) as are also ↓ vaqalapN and ↓ viqolapN and ↓ vaqolapN and ↓ viqalapN ; (K;) as meaning all the household-goods or furniture and utensils of persons going on a journey. (S, K.) ― -b2- See also viqolN . ― -b3- (assumed tropical:) The requisites and apparatus, instruments, tools, or the like, of a man: (Ham ubi suprà:) as, for instance, (tropical:) the books and writing-reeds of the learned man: every craftsman has what is thus termed. (TA.) By the saying kilaA vaqalayonaA TaAmiEN biganiymapK the author thereof, Iyás Et-Tá-ee, means Each of our two armies, the possessors of the vaqalaAni [or apparatus, or weapons, &c., of war, is longing for spoil ]: or an army may be termed vaqalN because it is heavy in assault. (Ham ubi suprà.) ― -b4- Anything held in high estimation, in much request, and preserved with care. (K, TA.) Hence the trad., A_in~iY taArikN fiykumu Alv~aqalayoni kitaAba A@ll~`hi waEitoratiY [ Verily I am leaving among you the two objects of high estimation and of care, the Book of God, and my kindred, or near kindred ]: (K:) or they are thus called because of the heaviness of acting in the manner required by them: (Th, TA:) or as being likened to the requisites and apparatus, instruments, tools, or the like, of a man. (Ham ubi suprà.) ― -b5- Also Eggs of the ostrich; because he who takes them rejoices in them, and they are food.
