Hence, i. e. from *im~apN in the first of the senses explained above, A^ahlu Al*~im~api , (S, Mgh, TA.) and Al*~im~ipu , (T, M, * Mgh, K, TA,) with the prefixed noun Ahl suppressed, (TA,) The people with whom a compact, or covenant, &c., has been made; (T, S, M, K, TA;) [and particularly] those, of the believers in a plurality of Gods, [by which are here meant the Christians, Jews, and Sabians, but no others,] who pay the [ tax called ] jizoyap ; (T, TA;) [i. e. the free non-Muslim subjects of a Muslim government, who pay a poll-tax for which the Muslims are responsible for their security and freedom and toleration: see A^aholN :] the appellation ↓ *im~iY~N , (Mgh, Msb,) a rel. n. from Al*~im~apu , (Msb;) is applied to a person of this class; (Mgh, Msb;) because he is rendered secure, or free from fear, for his property and his blood, by means of the jizoyap . (Mgh.) jaEala Eumaru A^ahola Als~awaAdi *im~apF means 'Omar treated [lit. made ] the people of the Sawád as those who are termed A^aholu Al*~im~api . (Mgh.) And A^aqobilonaA bi*im~apK [or A^aqolibonaA ?], in the prayer of the traveller, means Restore us to our family in safety. (TA.) It is related in a trad. of 'Alee, that he said, *im~atiY bimaA A^aquwlu rahiynapN wa A^anaA bihi zaEiymN , meaning My responsibility is pledged for [the truth of] what I say, and I am answerable for it; (Mgh, TA; *) i. e. this my saying is true, and I am responsible for it. (Mgh.) And it is said in another trad., faqado bariy^ato minohu Al*~im~ap [ Then the responsibility of God is clear, or quit, of him ]; i. e. there is given to every one, by God, a covenant whereby He binds Himself to preserve and protect him; and when he throws himself into destruction, or does that which is unlawful for him to do, or acts at variance with that which he is commanded to do, the covenant of God fails to aid him. (TA.) fiY *im~atiY ka*aA means fY DamaAniY [virtually I am responsible for such a thing; i. e. for paying it, or restoring it, &c.; but lit. in my responsibility is such a thing; or on my responsibility rests, or lies, or be, such a thing; for fY may be here used, as it is in many other instances, in the sense of EalaY ]: (Msb:) [or,] in the saying vabata fiY *im~atiY ka*aA , [which means Such a thing became, or has become, binding, obligatory, or incumbent, on me, ] the term *im~ap is applied to designate [the moral sense considered as ] the seat [ of the sense ] of obligation to fulfil what is [ properly ] termed *im~ap [i. e. a compact, or covenant, or the like ]. (Mgh.) Alr~aDaAEi ↓ maA yu*ohibu Ean~iY ma*im~apa (T, S, Mgh, *) or Alr~aDaAEi ↓ ma*am~apa , (T, Mgh,) meaning [ What will put away from me the obligation of ] the right, or due, of the woman who has suckled for the sucking? is a question occurring in a trad., (T, S, Mgh, *) as put by a man to the Prophet: (T:) and the answer was, “ A slave, male or female: ” (T, S, Mgh:) En-Nakha'ee says, (S,) they liked, on the occasion of the weaning of a child, to give the woman who had suckled it something beside the hire: (S, Mgh:) ↓ ma*am~apN in this case is a dial. var. of ↓ ma*im~apN : (Mgh:) or, as IAth says, the former is from Al*~am~u ; and the latter, from Al*~im~ahu . (TA.) You say also, Alr~aDaAEi bi$~aYo'K tuEoTiyhi ↓ A^a*ohibo Eanoka ma*am~a AlZ~iy^ora and Alr~aDaAEi ↓ ma*im~a , meaning [ Put away from thee the obligation of ] the right, or due, that is incumbent on thee to render her for the sucking of thy child [ by something that thou shalt give to her who has suckled ]. (T.) And A^a*ohibo Eanoka bi$aYo'K ↓ ma*im~atahumo and ↓ ma*am~atahumo , (T, and so accord. to different copies of the S and K, in which Enk is omitted,) ma*am~ap being a dial. var., (T,) i. e. [ Put away from thee the obligation of their right, or due, by something; meaning] feed them with something, (T,) or give to them something, (S, K,) for they have a right, or due. (T, S, K.) And ↓ qaDaY ma*im~atahu and ↓ ma*am~atahu [ He paid his right, or due; ] meaning he did good to him, or conferred upon him a benefit or benefits, in order that he might not be blamed. (M, K.) And rajulN ↓ *uw ma*im~apK and ↓ ma*am~apK [in the CK the latter only, A man who has a right, or due, ] meaning kal~N EalaY Aln~aAsi (tropical:) [ a man who is a burden upon people, to be maintained, or supported, by them ]. (M, K, TA.) -A2- Also (i. e. *im~apN ) A repast, or banquet, to which guests are invited, [ simply ] for food, or for a wedding. (K.) -A3- See also *am~apN .

Also, said of a thing, (T,) of a kaEob [i. e. cockal-bone, or die], [aor. and] inf. n. as above, (S, M, A, TA,) and of a man, (M, TA,) aor. as above, inf. n. ratobN , (M,) or ratabN , (K, * TA,) It, and he, stood erect, or upright; (T, S, M, A, TA; [but in some copies of the K, AlAinoSibaAbu is erroneously put for AlAinotiSaAbu as the explanation of Alr~atabu ;]) and (TA) so ↓ Artb , (K, TA, [but this I rather think to be a mistranscription,]) said of a man: mentioned in the T as on the authority of IAar. (TA. [But in the T, I find only rataba in this sense.]) So in the saying, rataba rutuwba AlkaEobi fiY AlmaqAmi AlS~aEobi [ He stood erect like as does the cockal-bone, or the die, in the difficult standingplace ]: (S, * A, TA:) occurring in a trad. of Lukmán Ibn-'Ád. (TA.) And rataba fiY AlS~alaApi He stood erect in prayer. (A.) [Or] rataba said of a man, [aor. ,] inf. n. ratobN and rutuwbN , signifies He remained, stayed, dwelt, or abode, in the town, or country: and also he stood firm. (Msb.) And you say also, rataba fiY AlA^amori [ He was constant, firm, &c., in the affair ]. (A.)

definition: , (S, M, A, &c.,) inf. n. tarotiybN , (S, K,) He made, or rendered, (a thing, S, M, or things, A,) constant, firm, steady, steadfast, stable, fixed, fast, settled, established, and stationary, or...
sourceDefinition: , (S, M, A, &c.,) inf. n. tarotiybN , (S, K,) He made, or rendered, (a thing, S, M, or things, A,) constant, firm, steady, steadfast, stable, fixed, fast, settled, established, and stationary, or motionless. (S, * M, Msb, K.) You say, rt~b AlT~alaAy^iEa fiY AlmaraAtibi [ He stationed the scouts upon the mrAtb ]. (A. See marotabapN .) ― -b2- He set things in order, disposed them regularly, arranged them, or classified them. (MA.) You say, rt~b Alr~utaba [ He set in order, regularly disposed, arranged, classified, distributed, or appointed, the stations, posts of honour, &c.]. (TA voce A^aS~ala .) ― -b3- [Hence,] tarotiybN is sometimes used as signifying The mode of construction termed laf~N wana$orN [ when it is regularly disposed: see art. lf ]. (Har p. 383.) ― -b4- [Also The prescribing, or observing, a particular order in any performance; as, for instance, in the ablution termed AlwuDuwo' .] ― -b5- And The drawing of omens, one after another. (KL.)

definition: The steps of stairs.
sourceDefinition: The steps of stairs. (M, TA.) ― -b2- Rocks near together, some of them higher than others: (M, K:) [a coll. gen. n.:] n. un. ↓ ratabapN ; mentioned on the authority of Yaakoob as [written ↓ rutabN ,] with damm to the r and fet-h to the t . (M.) ― -b3- Elevated ground, (S, K,) like a barozax [or bar, or an obstruction, between two things: app. a coll. gen. n. in this sense also; n. un. with p ; for] you say ↓ ratabapN and ratabN like as you say darajapN and darajN . (S.) ― -b4- Hardness, or difficulty: (S, A, K:) coarseness, hardness, or difficulty, of life or living: (M, K: *) fatigue, weariness, embarrassment, or trouble; as also ↓ marotabapN . (M.) You say, maA fiY Eayo$ihi ratabN (T, S, M, A) There is no hardness, or difficulty, in his life or living: (S, A:) or no coarseness, hardness, or difficulty. (M.) And maA fiY h`*aA AlA^amori ratabN , and ↓ marotabapN , There is no fatigue, weariness, embarrassment, or trouble, in this affair. (M.) And maA fiY h`*aA AlA^amori ratabN walA EatabN There is not in this affair any hardness, or difficulty: (S:) or any fatigue, or trouble: (T:) i. e. it is easy, and rightly disposed. (T, A.) -A2- Also The space between the little finger and that next to it, namely, the third finger, [ when they are extended apart: ] and the space between the third finger and the middle finger [ when they are so extended ]: (M, K:) or the space between the fore finger and the middle finger [ when they are so extended ]: sometimes written and pronounced ↓ ratobN : (S, TA:) [or it is a coll. gen. n.; and] ↓ ratabapN [is the n. un., and] signifies the space between [ any two of ] the fingers. (TA in art. rtq . [See also buSomN .]) It denotes also The [ space that is measured by ] putting the four fingers close together. (K. [See also EatabN .])

definition: A single step of stairs or of a ladder;
sourceDefinition: A single step of stairs or of a ladder; (MA;) [and so ↓ marotabapN , as appears from what follows:] pl. of the former rutabN (MA) [and rutabaAtN , for Az says that] rutobapN signifies one of the rutabaAt of stairs: (T:) [the pl. of marotabapN is maraAtibu .] You say, raqiYa fiY rutabi Ald~araji and ↓ maraAtibihaA [ He ascended the steps of the stairs ]. (A.) ― -b2- [Hence,] also, (S, M, A, * Msb, K,) and ↓ marotabapN , (T, S, M, A, K, TA,) [or] from rataba signifying “ he stood erect, ” (TA,) (tropical:) A station, or standing; a post of honour; rank; condition; degree; dignity; or office; (T, S, M, A, Msb, K, TA;) with, or at the courts of, kings; and the like: (T, TA:) or a high station, &c.: (TA:) pl. of the former rutabN ; (A, * Msb, TA;) and of the latter ↓ maraAtibu . (A, TA.) You say, huwa fiY A^aEolaY Alr~utabi (tropical:) [ He is in the highest of stations, &c.]: and Einoda ↓ lahu marotabapN Als~uloTaAni (tropical:) [ He has a station, &c., or high station, &c., with, or at the court of, the Sultán ]: and ↓ huwa mino A^aholi AlmaraAtibi (tropical:) [ He is of the people of high stations, &c.]. (A, TA.) ― -b3- [ rutobapN also signifies The order of the proper relative places of things; as, for instance, of the words in a sentence.] ― -b4- See also the pl. rutabN in the next preceding paragraph.

sourceDefinition: (Msb) and ↓ turotubN and ↓ turotabN (M, K) and ↓ tarotubN (M) A thing constant, firm, steady, steadfast, stable, fixed, fast, settled, established, stationary, or motionless: (M, Msb, K: [the third of these words, in this sense, is mentioned in the T in art. trb : but see the next paragraph:]) and the first, standing erect, or upright; (T, TA;) applied to a thing, (T,) to a kaEob [i. e. cockal-bone, or die], and to a man. (TA.) You say A^amorN raAtibN A thing, or an affair, continual, or uninterrupted, ( daAr~N .) constant, firm, steady, &c.: and ↓ A^amorN turotabN , the latter word of the measure tufoEalN , with damm to the t and fet-h to the E , a thing, or an affair, constant, firm, steady, &c. (S.) And Eiz~N raAtibN Might, high rank or condition, or the like, constant, firm, &c. (A.) And Eayo$N raAtibN Constant, or continual, (M, TA,) fixed, settled, or established, (TA,) means of subsistence. (M, TA.) And maA zilotu EalaY h`*aA raAtibFA I ceased not to be, or to do, thus constantly; as also raAtimFA ; in which, IJ says, the m is app. a substitute for b , because we have not heard ratama used like rataba ; but it may be radical, from Alr~atiymapu . (M.) ― -b2- [ raAtibN in the modern language, used as a subst., signifies A set pension, salary, and allowance; a ration; and any set office, or task: and so raAtibapN ; pl. rawaAtibu .]

definition: and turotubN and tarotubN : see the next preceding paragraph, in four places.
sourceDefinition: and turotubN and tarotubN : see the next preceding paragraph, in four places. ― -b2- You say also, jaAw^uwA turotabFA and turotubFA , meaning They came all together. (K.) And a poet says, (M,) namely, Ziyád Ibn-Zeyd El-'Odharee, (TA,) wakaAna lanaA faDolN EalaY Aln~aAsi turotabaA meaning [ And we possessed excellence above the people ] all together: (M, TA:) thus accord. to the reading commonly known: but, as some relate it, wakaAna lanaA Haq~FA EalaY Aln~aAsi turotabaA i. e. [ And it was a just claim that we had upon the people, ] settled, or established. (TA.) The first t in turotabN is augmentative, because there is no word like juEofarN ; and the derivation also is an evidence of this, for the word is from Al$~aYo'u Alr~aAtibu . (M.) ― -b2- Also the second, (Th, M, K,) and the first, (K,) Dust, or earth; syn. turaAbN : (Th, M, K:) because of its long endurance. (Th, M.) ― -b3- And the first, i. q. definition: A certain disease which attacks camels, in the rump;
sourceDefinition: A certain disease which attacks camels, in the rump; (S, K;) so that when a she-camel rises, or is roused, her thighs tremble for a while, and then stretch out: (S:) or it is when there is a convulsive motion in the hind leg or the thighs of a camel, when he desires to stand up, or rises, or is roused, for a while, and then a stretching out of the same. (TA.) -A2- Hence, (S,) Alr~ajazu is the name of A certain species [or kind ] of verse or poetry; (S, A, K;) a species [or kind ] of the metres of verse; (Msb;) consisting of the measure musotafoEiluno [ primarily ] six times: (K:) a metre easy to the ear and impressive to the mind; wherefore it may be reduced to a single hemistich, and also to two feet instead of six: (TA:) so called because it commences with a motion and a quiescence, [i. e., a movent and a quiescent letter,] followed by a motion and a quiescence; and so in the other feet; resembling the rajaz in a she-camel, which consists in her quivering and then being quiet: (TA:) or because of the contractedness of its feet, and the fewness of its letters: (S, K:) or because it is [characterized by] Suduwr without A^aEojaAz [lit. breasts without rumps; for, as the two hemistichs generally rhyme with each other, the verse seems as though it had no Eajuz ; i. e., as though its last foot should rather be called EaruwDN , like the last of the first hemistich, than EajuzN :] (TA:) Akh once said, rajazN , with the Arabs, is whatever consists of three feet; and it is that [kind of verse] which they sing in their work, and in driving their camels: [see bi*olapN , last sentence:] ISd says that certain of those in whom he placed confidence related this on the authority of Kh. (TA.) Some say that it is not verse, or poetry, but a kind of rhyming prose; but Kh held it to be true verse, or poetry: so in the M: but in the T it is said [as in the K] that Kh asserted it to be not poetry, but halves or thirds of verses: one of his reasons for this assertion [the only one that seems to have had much weight with the Muslims] is, that Mo- hammad once said, A^anaA A@bonu Eabodi AlmuT~alibo A^anaA Aln~abiY~u laA ka*ibo [which is an instance of a species of rajaz , meaning, “ I am the Prophet: it is no lie: I am the son of 'Abd-el-Muttalib ”]: and were this verse, he would not have said it, as is shown by what is said in the Kur., xxxvi. 69: but on this point, Akh has contended against him. (TA.)

Each of them composed a complete deewán of rajaz .] ― -b2- [Hence,] ↓ saHaAbapN raj~aAzapN (tropical:) [ A cloud thundering much, or uninterruptedly ]. (A, TA.) And ↓ gayovN murotajizN , and ↓ mutaraj~izN , (tropical:) Rain accompanied by thunder. (TA.)

definition: A camel having the disease termed rajazN : fem.
sourceDefinition: A camel having the disease termed rajazN : fem. rajozaA='u : (S, K:) the latter is explained as signifying weak in the rump, that does not move from her place unless after twice or thrice rising from the place where she lay: and that does not rise, when she desires to do so, unless after vehement trembling. (TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] A_in~ahaA larajozaA='u , said of the wind ( Alr~iyH ), (assumed tropical:) Verily it is continuous, or lasting. (TA.) And rajozaA='u AlqiyaAmi (tropical:) A great, heavy cooking-pot. (TA.)

definition: A well-known mikoyaAl [or measure with which corn is measured ], (T,) a large mikoyaAl , (S, M, K,) in Egypt, (K,) [i.
sourceDefinition: A well-known mikoyaAl [or measure with which corn is measured ], (T,) a large mikoyaAl , (S, M, K,) in Egypt, (K,) [i. e.] of the people of Egypt; (T, S;) or a certain measure of capacity well known in Egypt; (Msb;) not correctly called a mikoyaAl for they do not measure with it, but with the wayobap : (IB, TA:) it comprises, ( yaDum~u , [so in the M, but in copies of the K wayuDam~u , which signifies that it is also pronounced with damm,]) as they say, (M,) or it takes, (T,) twenty-four times the measure called SaAE , (T, M, Msb, K,) of wheat, (T,) i. e. sixty-four times the measure called man~ , (T, Msb,) the mn~ here meant being the mn~ of our country, (Az, [app. meaning El-'Irák,]) and the SAE being that of the Prophet: (Msb:) or six wayobaAt : (K:) the Ardb~ of Egypt is six wayobaAt ; the wayobap being four A^arobaAE ; the ruboE , four A^aqodaAH ; and the qadaH , two hundred and thirty-two daraAhim : (EsSuyootee in his “ Husn el-Mohádarah:”) the half of the Ardb~ is called qanoqalN : (T:) the word Ardb~ is affirmed by some to be arabicized: (MF:) [it is now vulgarly pronounced A^arodab~ :] the pl. is A^araAdibu . (Msb.) El-Akhtal says, qawomN A_i*aA A@sotanobaHa AlA^aDoyaAfu kalobahumu qaAluwA liA^um~ihimu buwliY EalaY Aln~aAri waAlxubozu kaAlEanobari AlhinodiY~i Einodahumu waAlqamoHu saboEuwna A_irodab~FA bidiynaAri [ Persons who, when the guests induce their dog to bark, (see art. nbH ,) say to their mother, “ Make water on the fire: ” and bread is like Indian ambergris in their judgment, while wheat is seventy irdebbs for a deenár ]: the former of these two verses [whereof the latter only is cited in the S] is said by As and others to be the most severely-satirical verse uttered by any of the Arabs. (TA.) ― -b2- Also A conduit in which water flows upon the surface of the ground. (M, K.)

definition: and radogapN Slime, or mire;
sourceDefinition: and radogapN Slime, or mire; i. e. water and clay or mud: and stiff slime or mire: (S, K:) or much slime or mire: (JK:) pl. ridaAgN and [coll. gen. ns.] ↓ radagN (S, K) and ↓ radogN : (K:) or ↓ ridaAgN signifies thin mud: or, as some say, it is pl. of radogapN : (Mgh:) accord. to Kr, ↓ radogN and ↓ ridaAgN signify slime, or mire; and are sings. (TA.) [See also razagapN .] Hence, ↓ yawomN *uw radogK [ A day of slime, or mire, &c.]. (TA, from a trad.) And Eani AljumuEapi ↓ manaEanaA h`*aA Alr~idaAgu [ This slime, or mire, &c., prevented us from attending the prayer of Friday: AlrdAg being here used as a sing. n.]. (TA, from another trad.) ― -b2- [Hence also,] radogapu AlxabaAli and radagapu AlxbAl The [ corrupt ] fluid squeezed, or wrung, or flowing, from the inhabitants of Hell. (K, TA.) This, it is said in a trad., will be given to drink to him who drinks wine. (TA.) ― -b3- You say also maA='N radogapN and radagapN [app. Slimy, or miry, water ]; both meaning the same. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: A rawoDap [i. e. meadow, or garden, ] that is beautiful, or goodly; or that is beautiful in appearance, exciting admiration, and satisfying the eye: (IAar, K:) and so marogadapN . (TA.) -A2- Also sing. of maraAdigu , which signifies The parts between the neck and the collar-bone: (S, K;) also called the baA=dil . (S.) And The portion of flesh [or muscle ] between the waAbilap of the katif [i. e. the extremity in which is the glenoid cavity of the shoulder-blade, or the muscle of the shoulderblade, ] and the heads of the ribs of the breast: (IAar, K:) or the maraAdig are [the parts ] beneath the two collar-bones, on each side of the breast. (TA.) And you say naAqapN *aAtu maraAdiga (K) and jamalN *uw maraAdiga (TA) meaning A fat she-camel (K) and he-camel: (TA:) ISh says, when the camel is satisfied by abundance of herbage, he has mrAdg in his belly and upon the upper parts of his shoulder-blades, i. e. accumulated fat thereon, like hares lying down; but when he is not fat, there is no ↓ marodag there. (TA.) marodagapu AlEunuqi means A portion of flesh [or a muscle, app. of a camel,] upon the hinder side of the rising part from the middle of the EaDud [or humerus ] to the elbow: or, as some say, the flesh of the breast. (TA.) And maraAdigu Als~anaAmi means The fat that adjoins the maA^onap [q. v., of the hump ]: (JK, Ibn- 'Abbád, TA:) sing. marodagapN . (JK.)

definition: , (S, * A, K,) and rakiba Ealayohi , (A,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, * A, K,) and rakiba Ealayohi , (A,) aor. , (A, K,) inf. n. rukuwbN (S, A, K) and marokabN ; (A, K;) and ↓ Artkbhu ; (K;) I. q. EalaAhu (A, K, TA) and EalaA Ealayohi [explained by what follows]. (TA.) You say, rakibotu Ald~aAb~apa , (Msb,) or Alfarasa , (Mgh,) and rakibotu EalayohaA , [or Ealayohi ,] inf. n. rukuwbN and marokabN [as above, meaning I rode, or rode upon, and I mounted, or mounted upon, the beast, or the horse ]. (TA. [See also raAkibN .]) [And rakibotu Als~afiynapa , or fiY Als~afiynapi (agreeably with the Kur xi. 43 and xviii. 70 and xxix. 65), I embarked in the ship; went on board the ship. ] And one says, of anything, rakibahu [and ↓ Artkbh ] as meaning EalaAhu [i. e. (assumed tropical:) It was, or became, upon, or over, it; got upon it; came, or arose, upon it; overlay it; was, or became, superincumbent, or supernatant, upon it; overspread it ]; namely, another thing. (TA.) [In like manner,] one says also, of anything, rukiba and ↓ Aurotukiba as meaning EuliYa [i. e., when said of a horse or the like, He was ridden, or ridden upon, and was mounted, or mounted upon: whence other significations in other cases, indicated above]. (TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] rakiba baEoDuhu baEoDFA i. q. ↓ trAkb (tropical:) [ It lay one part upon another; it was, or became, heaped, or piled, up, or together, one part upon, or overlying, another: ] said of fat [as meaning it was, or became, disposed in layers, one above another: see raAkibapN ]. (A, TA.) [And hence, rakiba Aln~aAsu baEoDuhumo baEoDFA (assumed tropical:) The people bore, or pressed, or crowded, ( as though mounting, ) one upon another; a phrase well known, and of frequent occurrence: or meaning (assumed tropical:) the people followed one another closely; from what next follows.] ― -b3- rakibahu also means [(assumed tropical:) He came upon him, or overtook him; or] he followed closely, or immediately, after him: and rakibotu A^avarahu and Tariyqahu (assumed tropical:) I followed close after him. (L.) ― -b4- [ rakiba AlT~ariyqa , and Alr~amola , and AlmafaAzapa , (assumed tropical:) He went upon, or trod, or travelled, the road, and the sand or sands, and the desert: and rakiba AlbaHora (assumed tropical:) He embarked, or voyaged, upon the sea. sourceDefinition: , [inf. n. as below,] He lent him the horse, [or mounted him on the horse, ] to go forth on a warring and plundering expedition, on the condition of receiving from him one half of the spoil: (K, * TA:) or for a portion of the spoil that he should obtain. (TA.) [See also 4.] ― -b2- And rk~bhu , inf. n. tarokiybN , He put, or set, one part of it upon another: (K:) [ he set it, or fixed it, in another thing: he composed it; constituted it; or put it together. ] tarokiybN signifies The putting together, or combining, things, whether suitable or not, or placed in order or not: it is a more general term than taA^oliyfN , which is the collecting together, or putting together, suitable things. (Kull p. 118.) You say, rak~aba AlfaS~a fiY AlxaAtami (S, A) He set the stone in the signet-ring: and rk~b Als~inaAna fiY AlqanaApi He fixed the spearhead in the shaft; (A;) and Aln~aSola fiY Als~ahomi [ the arrow-head in the shaft ]. (S.) And $aYo'N Hasanu Alt~arokiybi [ A thing good, or beautiful, in respect of composition or constitution; well, or beautifully, composed or constituted or put together ]. (TA.) ― -b3- Also He removed it from one place to another in which to plant it; namely, a shoot of a palm-tree. (Mgh.)

definition: A single ride, or act of riding: pl.
sourceDefinition: A single ride, or act of riding: pl. rakabaAtN . (IAth, L.) ― -b2- [Hence,] one says, huwa yamo$iY Alr~akobapa (tropical:) [i. e. yarokabu raA^osahu He goes at random, heedlessly, or in a headlong manner, &c., (see 1,)] and humo yamo$uwna Alr~akabaAti (tropical:) [ They go at random, &c.]. (A. [The meaning is there indicated by the context, and is shown by what here follows.]) Respecting the phrase tmo$uwna Alr~akabaAti , occurring in a trad., meaning tarokabuwna ruw^uwsakumo (assumed tropical:) [ Ye go at random, &c.], in that which is false, wrong, or vain, and in factions, or seditions, or the like, following one another without consideration, IAth says that rakobapN [properly] signifies as explained above in the first sentence of this paragraph, and that the pl. AlrkbAt is here governed in the accus. case by a verb understood, and [with that verb] is a denotative of state relating to the agent in tm$wn : it supplies the place of that verb, which it does not require to be expressed; and the implied meaning is tamo$uwna tarokabuwna Alr~akabaAti . (L.)

[The meaning is there indicated by the context, and is shown by what here follows.]) Respecting the phrase tmo$uwna Alr~akabaAti , occurring in a trad., meaning tarokabuwna ruw^uwsakumo (assumed tropical:) [ Ye go at random, &c.], in that which is false, wrong, or vain, and in factions, or seditions, or the like, following one another without consideration, IAth says that rakobapN [properly] signifies as explained above in the first sentence of this paragraph, and that the pl. AlrkbAt is here governed in the accus. case by a verb understood, and [with that verb] is a denotative of state relating to the agent in tm$wn : it supplies the place of that verb, which it does not require to be expressed; and the implied meaning is tamo$uwna tarokabuwna Alr~akabaAti . (L.)

definition: a word of well-known meaning, (S, Msb,) [The knee;
sourceDefinition: a word of well-known meaning, (S, Msb,) [The knee; i. e., in a man,] the joint between the lower parts of the thigh and the upper parts of the shank: (A, K:) or [in a quadruped,] the joint between the metacarpus and the radius ( mawoSilu AlwaZiyfi waAl*~iraAEi ): this is the right explanation: in the K, mawoDiE is erroneously put for mawoSil : [this explanation is evidently given accord. to the terms employed in the anatomy of quadrupeds as compared to human beings: in that which next follows, there is certainly an omission, which I have endeavoured to supply:] or the rukobataAni of the fore legs of the camel are the two joints that [ project forwards, in like manner as do, in the hind legs, those that ] are next the belly [meaning the stifle-joints ] when he lies down upon his breast with folded legs: the two joints that project behind [in the hind legs, namely, the hocks,] are called the EuroquwbaAni : in every quadruped, the rkbtAn are in the fore legs, and the ErqwbAn are in the hind legs: and the Erqwb is what is called mawoSilu AlwaZiyfi [i. e. the upper joint of the metatarsus]: (TA:) or the rkbp is the mirofaq [which in a man is the elbow, but here seems to mean the lower joint ] of the *iraAE [or radius ] of anything [i. e. of any beast]: (K:) [from its being said in the S and Msb that the rukobap is “ well known, ” I conclude that there is no real discrepancy in the foregoing explanations: it is perhaps needless to add that the term rukobap is now universally applied to the knee of a man and to what we commonly call the knee of a horse and the like:] the pl. is rukabN , (S, Msb, K,) i. e. the pl. of mult., and the pl. of pauc. is rukobaAtN and rukabaAtN and rukubaAtN . (S.) Lh mentions the phrase baEiyrN musotawoqiHu Alr~ukabi [meaning A hardkneed camel ]; as though the term rukobapN were applied to each part, and the pl. used accord. to this application. (TA.) ― -b2- One says [of an agitating affair or event], A^amorN A@SoTak~ato fiyhi Alr~ukabu waHak~ato fiyhi Alr~ukobapu Alr~ukabapa (tropical:) [ An affair, or event, in which the knees knocked together, and in which the knee rubbed the knee ]. (A.) ― -b3- And of one who has the mark of prostration in prayer on his forehead, between his eyes, (L,) bayona Eayonayohi mivolu rukobapi AlEanozi [ Between his eyes is the like of the knee of the she-goat ]. (A, * L.) And of any two things that are alike, or correspondent, humaA karukobataY AlEanozi [ They are like the two knees of the she-goat ]; because her two knees fall together upon the ground when she lies down. (L.) ― -b4- And it is said in a prov., $ar~u Aln~aAsi mano miloHuhu EalaY rukEbatihi [ The worst of men is he whose fat is upon his knee ]: applied to him who is quickly angered; and to the perfidious: (Meyd, TA:) the phrase miloHuhu EalaY rukobatihi is also used as meaning The smallest thing makes him angry: (TA:) and a poet says, laA talumohaA A_in~ahaA mino EuSobapK miloHuhaA mawoDuwEapN fawoqa Alr~ukabo [ Blame her not; for she is of a set of people whose fat is placed above the knees: perhaps meaning, for she is but a woman; as women are generally fat in the part above the knee]: (TA:) or mino nisowapK [in the place of mino EuSobapK ], meaning of women whose object of anxiety, or care, is fatness and fat: (Meyd, TA:) so that the prov. seems to mean that the worst of men is he who has not such intelligence as bids him to do that which is praiseworthy, but only bids him to do that in which is inconstancy and levity, and an inclining to the dispositions of women, to the love of fatness and fat. (Meyd.) [See other explanations in art. mlH .] -A2- Also The lower part ( A^aSol ) of the plant Sil~iyaAnap , when it has been cut. (K.)

definition: [ Travelling-camels, used for riding;
sourceDefinition: [ Travelling-camels, used for riding; i. e.] camels (S, K, TA) upon which people journey; (S, TA;) i. q. maTiY~N : (Msb:) or camels fit for carrying: (Har p. 22:) it has no proper sing.: (S:) the word used for the sing. is raAHilapN : (S, Msb, K:) or, as ISh says, in the “ Book of Camels, ” rikaAbN and EiyrN are applied to camels that go forth for corn ( TaEaAm ) to be brought back upon them, both when they go forth and after they have come back: and the former term is applied also to camels upon which people journey to Mekkeh, on which maHaAmil are borne: and hired [or other ] camels that carry the goods and corn of merchants: but camels are not called Eyr , though bearing corn, [unless] if hired: [I insert the words “ or other ” and “ unless ” because it is further said,] Eyr are not those that bring corn for their owners; but these are called rikaAbN : (L, TA:) the pl. is rukubN , (S, K,) accord. to A'Obeyd, (TA,) and rikaAbaAtN and rakaAy^ibu ; (K;) or, accord. to IAar, rukubN is not pl. of rikaAbN ; and others say that it is pl. of ↓ rakuwbN , signifying any beast on which one rides, [an epithet] of the measure faEuwlN in the sense of the measure mafoEuwlN ; (TA;) but called by ISd a subst.; (TA voce jazuwzN ;) and ↓ rakuwbapN is a more special term than rakuwbN . (TA in the present art.) ― -b2- [Hence,] rikaAbu Als~aHaAbi (tropical:) [ The bearers of the clouds; i. e.] the winds. (A, K.) Umeiyeh says, tarad~adu waAlr~iyaAHu lahaA rikaAbu [ It (referring to a cloud) goes to and fro ( tarad~ad being for tatarad~adu ), the winds being its bearers ]. (TA.) -A2- Also [The stirrup of a horse's saddle;] a well-known appertenance of a horse's saddle; (S;) the same with respect to a horse's saddle as the garoz with respect to a camel's: pl. rukubN . (K.)

(TA.) ― -b3- And TariyqN rakuwbN A road ridden upon, (S, TA,) and trodden so as to be rendered even, or easy to be travelled. (TA.) -A2- See also rak~aAbN .

sourceDefinition: Riding; or a rider: (Mgh, Msb, K:) or properly only a rider upon a camel: (ISk, S, K:) or the latter is its meaning when it is not used as a prefixed noun, as explained below; and is said to be the original signification: IB says that it may signify a rider upon a camel, ass, horse, or mule, when used as a prefixed noun; as when you say riAkibu jamalK and raAkibu HimaArK &c.: (L:) accord. to ISk, you term a rider upon an ass faArisN EalaY HimaArK , (S, TA,) and a rider upon a mule faArisN EalaY bagolK ; (TA;) but 'Omarah says, I do not call the owner or rider of the ass fArs , but Ham~aArN ; and the reason of his saying so is manifest, for fArs is an epithet of the measure faAEilN from Alfarasu “ the horse, ” meaning “ an owner, or a rider, of the horse: ” (S, TA:) the pl. is ruk~aAbN (S, K) and rukobaAnN (S, * Mgh, Msb, K) and rukuwbN (Mgh, K) and rikabapN , (K,) or this last is a mistake for rakabapN [q. v.], (MF, TA,) and ↓ rakobN , (Akh, Msb, K, TA,) as some say; (TA;) or this last is a quasi-pl. n., (K, TA,) not a broken pl. of raAkibN ; (TA;) and signifies riders upon camels; (K;) or owners of camels on a journey, or travellers upon camels; (S;) consisting of ten or more: (S, K:) and sometimes it signifies riders upon horses: (IB, K:) or riders upon horses and camels: (IB, L, TA:) or a company of riders upon horses; or upon horses and camels: (TA:) [or, accord. to Kh, riders upon any beasts: (De Sacy's Anthol. Gram. Ar. p. 54 of the Arabic text:)] in the Kur viii. 43, Alr~akobu may signify the riders upon horses, or the riders upon camels, or the army composed of both these: (TA:) the pl. of rakobN is A^arokubN , (S, K,) [a pl. of pauc.,] and rukuwbN . (K.) Accord. to IB, you do not say A_ibilK ↓ rakobu nor rukobaAnu A_ibilK : but it is said that ruk~aAbu A_ibilK and ruk~aAbu xayolK &c. are allowable. (L.) An instance of rukobaAn as distinguished from furosaAn occurs in a verse cited as one of the exs. of the preposition bi . (TA.) ↓ rukayobN [properly signifying A small company of riders upon camels, &c.,] occurs as meaning collectors of the poorrates: it is the dim. of ↓ rakobN ; and shows that this latter is not a pl. [properly speaking] of raAkibN ; for, were it so, the word used as its dim. would be ruwayokibuwna . (TA.) [See also rakabapN , and A^urokuwbN .] ― -b2- [Also A person on board of a ship or boat: pl. ruk~aAbN .] You say ruk~aAbu Als~afiynapi (S, TA) The persons on board of the ship, or boat: and ruk~aAbu AlmaA='i the voyagers upon the water: and Ibn-Ahmar has used in this sense the pl. rukobaAnN ; but it is said that this is not allowable; nor is A^urokuwbN ; nor rakobN . (TA.) ― -b3- Also, and ↓ raAkuwbN , (assumed tropical:) A shoot germinating upon the trunk of a palm-tree, not having any root in the ground: (S:) or a shoot on the upper part of a palm-tree, hanging down, but not reaching the ground; and so ↓ raAkibapN and ↓ raAkuwbapN and ↓ rak~aAbapN : (K:) or, as some say, the last of these words is not thus applied, but means a woman “ who rides much: ” AHn, however, says that it signifies a palm-shoot, or the like thereof, growing forth at the top of the trunk of a palm-tree, and, in some instances, bearing with its mother; but when it is cut off, it is better for the mother: and raAkibN is also explained in the L as meaning small palm-trees that grow forth at the lower parts of large palmtrees: (TA:) or it means a shoot of a palm-tree not cut off from its mother: (Ham p. 66:) accord. to As, when a palm-shoot grows from the trunk, and does not adhere to the ground, it forms a vile kind of palm-tree; and the Arabs call it raAkibN and ↓ raAkuwbN : the pl. of this last [and of ↓ raAkuwbapN ] is rawaAkiybu . (TA.) ― -b4- rukobaAnu Als~unobuli means (tropical:) What first appear, or grow forth, from the qunobuE , (A, K, TA,) i. e. the envelope of the grain, (TA,) of the ear of wheat. (K, TA.) ― -b5- raAkibN also signifies (assumed tropical:) The head [or summit ] of a mountain ( jabal ), as in [most of] the copies of the K; in some of which is found Habol [or rope ]. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: A man to whom a horse is lent for a portion of the spoil that he may obtain: (IAar, TA:) or a man who borrows a horse upon which to go forth on a warring and plundering expedition, and who receives one half of the spoil, the other half being for the lender: (K:) or one to whom a horse has been given for him to ride, and who has put his foot into the stirrup. (A.) [Also] Weak in the art of horsemanship, or the management of horses, and the riding of them. (Ham p. 441.) ― -b2- [Also Put, or set, one part upon another: set, or fixed, in another thing: composed; constituted; or put together: see its verb, 2.] The stone [ set ] in the signet-ring is termed murak~abN and ↓ rakiybN ; and so the arrowhead [ fixed ] in the shaft: (S:) or rakiybN signifies, (K, TA,) as a subst., (TA,) a thing set ( murak~abN ) in a thing, such as a ring-stone in the bezel, or collet, of the signet-ring. (K, * TA.) -A2- Also (tropical:) Origin: and place of growth or germination or vegetation. (S, K, TA.) You say, fulaAnN kariymu Almurak~abi (tropical:) Such a one is generous, or noble, in respect of the origin of his rank among his people. (S, A. *)

definition: Falling in drops.
sourceDefinition: Falling in drops. (AA, T, K.) ruwaAlN raAy^ilN means Slaver falling in drops. (AA, T.) And (K) it has an intensive signification, [app. meaning Much slaver, ] (M, K,) like $iEorN $aAEirN . (M.) -A2- Also, (M, K,) and ↓ raAwuwlN , (S, TA,) but disallowed in this sense by As, (T, S,) in the K, erroneously, ↓ ruwaAlN , (TA, [see also ruw^aAlN , in art. rA^l ,]) A redundant tooth, (S, M, K,) in a man and a horse, (S,) not growing in the manner of the A^aDoraAs [or other teeth ]: (M, K:) or raAy^ilN and ↓ raAy^ilapN signify a tooth that grows to a horse or similar beast, preventing him from drinking [ with ease ] and from [ eating in the manner termed ] qaDomN : (Lth, T:) accord. to ISh, rawaAy^ilu [pl. of ↓ raAy^ilapN ] signifies small teeth that grow at the roots of the large teeth, and excavate the roots of the latter so that these fall out: (T:) [and] so rawaAwiylu : (TA:) or this last, which is pl. of ↓ raAwuwlN , signifies redundant teeth that are behind the [ other ] teeth; as also rawaAwilu , with the Y elided. (Ham p. 818.)

sourceDefinition: Any [ covering for the body such as is called ] mulaA='ap not of two pieces (S, Mgh, Msb, K) joined together (Mgh, TA) by sewing or the like, (TA,) but a single piece, (S, K,) all one web: (K:) it is said by Az to be, without exception, white: (TA:) or it signifies, (Mgh, K,) or signifies also, sometimes, (Msb,) any garment, or piece of cloth, that is thin (Mgh, Msb, K) and soft; (Mgh, K;) so says ISk, on the authority of certain of the Arabs of the desert; (TA;) as also ↓ raAy^iTapN : (K:) and a napkin with which the hands are wiped after food: (TA, from a trad., expl. by Sufyán:) [in Har p. 294, q. v., it seems to be applied to a kind of woollen cloth used as a turban: ] pl. ↓ rayoTN [or this is rather a coll. gen. n. of which rayoTapN is the n. un.] and riyaATN . (S, Msb, K.) ― -b2- You say, xaraja mu$otamilFA birayoTapi AlZ~alomaA='i (tropical:) [ He went forth enveloped with the mantle of darkness ]. (TA.) And huwa yajur~u riyaATa AlHamodi (tropical:) [app. meaning He is prolix in praise ]. (TA.) ― -b3- The pl. riyaATN also signifies (assumed tropical:) Something resembling the saraAb [or mirage ] in the desert. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: is syn. with baraAHN ; (Lth, T, M, K;) and the verb is raAma , aor. yariymu , [ He went away, or departed; and he quitted a place: and he ceased doing a thing:] (Lth, T, TA:) rayomN being the inf. n. (TA.) IAar used to say, in relation [or reply] to the saying maA rimotu [ I did not go away, &c., or I have not gone away, &c.], balaY qado rimotu [ Nay, I did go away, &c., or I have gone away, &c.]: but others use the verb only with a negative particle: (T:) or it is mostly used in negative phrases. (TA.) You say, raAmahu , aor. yariymuhu , (S, Mgh,) inf. n. as above, (S,) He went away from it, departed from it, or quitted it; syn. bariHahu ; (S;) or zaAla minohu , and faAraqahu ; namely, his place. (Mgh.) And rimotu fulaAnFA and ramotu mino Einodi fulaAnK [ I went away from such a one ]: both meaning the same. (S.) And laA tarimohu Go not thou away from him, or it; syn. laAtaboraHohu . (S.) And maA rimotu AlmakaAna and maA rimotu minohu (M, K) I went not from the place; syn. maA bariHotu . (K.) And maA rimotu A^afoEalu *`lika (M, * K, * TA) I ceased not doing that; syn. maA bariHotu . (TA.) ― -b2- And i. q. tabaAEudN [The being, or becoming, distant, remote, far off, or aloof; &c.]: (T, K:) [you say,] maA yariymN [ He does not become distant, &c.]. (T.) [Accord. to the TK, it is, in this sense, inf. n. of raAmahu , aor. as above, meaning He was, or became, distant, &c., from it. ] ― -b3- And An inclining, or a leaning, in the load of a camel, (K, TA,) by reason of excess and heaviness thereof. (TA.) One says, lih`*aA AlEidoli rayomN EalaY h`*aA [ There is to this side-burden an inclining, or a leaning, by reason of an excess of weight over this: or,] a heaviness [ exceeding that of this ], by reason of which it inclines, or leans. (TA.) [And accord. to the TK, you say of the load of a camel, raAma , meaning It inclined, or leaned. ] ― -b4- And The becoming drawn together, of the mouth of a wound, in order to heal; as also rayamaAnN . (K.) [Both are said in the TK to be inf. ns. of raAma , aor. as above, said of a wound, meaning Its mouth became drawn together, in order to heal. ] -A2- riyma bihi i. q. quTiEa bihi [ He was or became, disabled from prosecuting, or unable to prosecute, his journey ]. (S, K.) A rájiz says, wariyma biAls~aAEiY Al~a*iY kaAna maEiY [ And the messenger that was with me became disabled from prosecuting his journey ]. (S, TA.)

One says, lih`*aA rayomN EalaY h`*aA This has excess, or superiority, ( faDolN , ISk, T,) over this. (ISk, T, S. *) Alr~ayomu EalaYAlmazojuwri , a phrase used by El-'Ajjáj, means mano zujira faEalayohi AlfaDolu [which may be rendered He who is chidden, it is incumbent on him to exceed; or he who is chidden is exceeded ]: (T, S:) such being always the case; for one is chidden only on account of an affair in which he has fallen short of doing what was requisite. (S.) ― -b2- A thing such as is termed EilaAwap [q. v.] between the two side-loads of a camel. (IAar, T, K.) Hence the saying, Alr~ayomu A^avoqalu EalaY Ald~awaAb~i mina AlHimoli [ The additional burden that is put between the two side-loads is more onerous to the beasts than the (usual) load ]. (TK) after the flesh of the slaughtered camel has been distributed (T, S) in the game called Almayosir , (T,) and which is given to the slaughterer: (M, K:) accord. to Lh, the camel for slaughter is brought, and its owner slaughters it, then puts it upon something laid upon the ground to preserve it from pollution, having divided it into ten portion, namely, the two haunches, and the two thighs, and the rump, and the withers, and the breast, and [ the part of the back called ] the maloHaA=' [q. v.], and the two shoulders together with the two arms; then he betakes himself to the TafaATif [or soft parts, such as the flanks, or the soft parts of the belly ], and the vertebræ of the neck, and distributes them upon those portions equally; and if there remain a bone, or a small piece of flesh, that is the rayom : then the slaughterer waits with it for him who desires it, and he whose arrow wins, his it is; otherwise, it is for the slaughterer. (M, TA.) ― -b3- The last portion of the day-time, extending to the confusedness ( AixotilaAT , for which AixotilaAf is erroneously put in the copies of the K, TA) of the darkness. (M, K, TA.) A long [ indefinite period such as is termed ] saAEap : (S, K:) so in the saying, qado baqiYa rayomN mina Aln~ahaAri [ A long period of the day-time had remained; or, emphatically, remains ]. (S.) And nahaArN rayomN means A long day or day-time: so in the saying, Ealayoka nahaArN rayomN [app. meaning A long day is appointed thee for the performance of a work or task]. (AZ, T.) -A2- Also i. q. darajapN [as meaning A series of stairs: ] (IAar, Jm, T, S, M, K:) of the dial. of El-Yemen. (S.) Aboo-'Amr Ibn-'Alà says, as related by As, I was in El-Yemen, and I came to the house of a man, inquiring for him, and a man of the house said to me, Ausomuko fiY Alr~ayomi , meaning AiSoEadi Ald~arajapi [ Ascend thou the stairs ]. (JM, cited in the PS.) ― -b2- And i. q. duk~aAnN [meaning A kind of wide bench, of stone or brick; and also a shop ]: (M, TA:) likewise of the dial. of El-Yemen. (TA.) ― -b3- And Small mountains. (IAar, T, K.) ― -b4- And A grave: (IAar, T, S, M, K:) or the middle thereof. (M, K.) -A3- See also what next follows.

definition: A woman who loves the discourse of men, but does not act vitiously or immorally, or commit adultery or fornication.
sourceDefinition: A woman who loves the discourse of men, but does not act vitiously or immorally, or commit adultery or fornication. (K.) Also a [female] proper name. (K.) definition: Embellishment, ornament, or decoration;
sourceDefinition: Embellishment, ornament, or decoration; consisting in variegated, or figured, work; or in jewels, or gems; (S, K, TA;) and the like: (S, TA:) embellishment, ornament, or decoration, of weapons: (TA:) and anything beautiful. (Th, TA.) [Hence,] ziboriju Ald~unoyaA The vanities and finery of the present world or state of existence. (TA, from a trad. of 'Alee.) ― -b2- Also Gold: (S, K:) so some say. (S.) ― -b3- And Thin clouds, in which is a redness: (Fr, S, K:) or clouds spotted in the surface with blackness and redness: or light clouds which the wind sweeps away, or disperses: or red clouds: but AZ says that the first of these is the correct signification: and clouds spotted like the leopard, seeming to be such as will give rain: and thin clouds, in which is no water. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , (S, K,) aor. yazojuw , (S,) inf. n. zajaA='N (S, K, and Ham p. 78) and zajowN (K and Ham) and zujuw~N , (K,) It (a thing) went, or became urged on or along, quickly. (Ham ubi suprà: there indicated by the context, but not expressed.) ― -b2- It (a bad piece of money) passed, or had currency. (Er-Rághib, TA.) ― -b3- It (an affair) was, or became, easy; and right, in a right state, or right in its direction or tendency. (K, TA.) Hence the trad., laA tazojuw SalaApN laA yuqoraA^u fiyhaA bifaAtiHapi AlkitaAbi i. e. [ A prayer in which the opening chapter of the Book (meaning the Kur-án) is not recited ] will not be right. (TA.) ― -b4- Also, inf. n. zajaA='N , said of the [tax called] xaraAj , It was, or became, easy of collection. (S.) ― -b5- zajaA='N also signifies The acting with penetrative energy, and effectiveness, in an affair. (S, K.) One says, h`*aA AlA^amoru qado zajawonaA Ealayohi [app. meaning This affair, we have effected it, or accomplished it; like as one says, maDayonaA EalaY AlA^amori ]. (T, TA.) And EaTaA='N qaliylN yazojuw xayorN mino kaviyrK laA yazojuw [ A small gift that is effective is better than much that will not be effective ]. (S.) -A2- One says also, DaHika Hat~aY zajaA i. e. [ He laughed until ] his laughing became stopped, or cut short. (S, K. *) -A3- See also what next follows, in two places.

definition: , (S, Msb, TA,) inf.
sourceDefinition: , (S, Msb, TA,) inf. n. tazojiyapN , (S, TA,) He pushed it gently, (S, Msb, TA,) in order that it might go on; as also ↓ AzjAhu ; and ↓ zajaAhu , aor. yazojuwhu , inf. n. zajowN : and this last, he drove it, or urged it on, gently; (TA;) [and so zj~Ahu and ↓ AzjAhu , as will be shown by what follows:] or ↓ zajaAhu signifies [simply] he drove it, or urged it on: and he pushed it: and so [app. in both of these senses] zj~Ahu and ↓ AzjAhu . (K.) Hence, i. e. from zaj~ayotuhu meaning “ I pushed it gently, ” (Har p. 304,) one says, kayofa tuzaj~iY AlA^ay~aAma (S, Har) i. e. kayofa tudaAfiEuhaA [ How dost thou strive with the days in pushing them on, or making them to pass away? ]: (S:) or kyf tadofaEuhaA [ how dost thou push on the days? and thus may mean also kyf tdAfEhA ]: (Har:) [or how dost thou make the days to pass away? for] zj~Y AlA^ay~aAma means he made the days to pass away: (MA:) [or how dost thou pass the days? for it is also said that] tazojiyapN signifies the passing [one's] days. (KL.) [ zj~Y AlA^ay~aAma may be well rendered He made the days to pass away by means of exertion; and so dafaEahaA and daAfaEahaA . Har (ubi suprà) uses the phrase A^uzaj~iY A^ay~aAmFA musowad~apF as meaning I push on evil and hard days. ] ↓ AzjY Al$~aYo'a , also, inf. n. A_izojaA='N , is expl. by Az as signifying daAfaEa biqaliylihi [app. meaning He strove to push on life, or to repel want or the like, with little of the thing ]: and accord. to a saying heard by him from a man of the tribe of Fezárah, nuzaj~iYdunoyaAnaA [or the correct reading may be ↓ nuzojiY , and accord. to either reading the phrase may be rendered We strive to push on life, or to repel want &c., with little of our worldly possessions, ] means we content ourselves in respect of our worldly possessions with scanty sustenance. (TA. [See also 5.]) One says also AlA_ibila ↓ A^azojayotu I drove the camels. (S.) And waladahaA ↓ Albaqarapu tuzojiY The [ wild ] cow drives her young one. (S.) Alr~iyHu Als~aHaAba ↓ tuzojiY The wind drives along the clouds: (S:) or drives along gently the clouds; as also tuzaj~iyhi , but in an intensive sense. (Msb.) In like manner, saHaAbFA ↓ yuzojiY is said of God, in the Kur [xxiv. 43]: and in the same [xvii. 68], rab~ukumu A@l~a*iY lakumu A@lofuloka fiY AlbaHori ↓ yuzojiY [ Your Lord is He who driveth along for you the ship in the sea ]. (TA.) And a poet says, ↓ zaj~ayotuhu biAlqawoli waA@zodajayotuhu i. e. [ I drove him with speech, and ] urged him on: for AizodajaAhu signifies saAqahu [like zaj~aAhu &c.]. (TA.) ― -b2- And zj~Y HaAjatiY He made easy the attainment of my want. (TA.) -A2- zj~Y Alr~umoHa i. q. A^azaj~ahu q. v. in art. zj . (TA in that art.)

sourceDefinition: , applied to a horse [or other beast], That is driven, or urged on, ( yzjY , [i. e. yuzojaY ,]) in his pace, by little and little. (Ham p. 158.) ― -b2- A small, or scanty, thing; (S, Er-Rághib, TA;) or such as is mean, or paltry; that may be pushed and driven away because of the little account that is made of it. (Er-Rághib, TA.) biDaAEapN muzojaApN means Small, or scanty, merchandise; little in quantity: (S, K:) and so it is said to mean in the Kur [xii. 88]: or, as in some copies of the S, little, or mean, or paltry, merchandise: (TA:) or mean, or paltry, merchandise, rejected by every one to whom it is offered: (A, TA:) or merchandise wherewith the days are pushed on ( tudofaEu [i. e. made to pass away by means of exertion ]) because of its scantiness: (Msb, TA: [for muzojaApN bihaA :]) or, accord. to the shereef El-Murtadà, merchandise driven along portion after portion, scantily and feebly: (TA:) or merchandise in respect of which a lowering of the price is demanded on account of its badness ( fiyhaA A_igomaADN ); (Th, TA;) not in perfect condition: (Th, K, TA:) thus, too, it is expl. as used in the Kur: and some say that what is there mentioned consisted of fruit of the terebinth-tree, or of Sanawobar [app. here meaning pine-cones]: some say, of commodities of the Arabs of the desert, wool, and clarified butter: and some say, of deficient pieces of money. (TA.)

definition: and zurobiY~N , (K,) or, accord.
sourceDefinition: and zurobiY~N , (K,) or, accord. to the L [and the A], on the authority of IAar, ↓ zarobiy~apN , also said to be written zirobiy~apN and zurobiy~apN , (TA,) are sings. of ↓ zaraAbiY~u , (K, TA,) which signifies namaAriqu [app. as meaning Small pillows ]: (S, A, K:) and carpets: or any things which are spread, and upon which one leans, or reclines: (A, K:) the like of this is said by Zj in explaining a phrase in which it occurs in the Kur lxxxviii. 16: or, accord. to Fr, it signifies carpets ( TanaAfis ) having a fine nap, or pile: (TA:) also, [particularly,] (A,) carpets ( quTuwE , A, or TanaAfis , Har p. 377) of the fabric of El- Heereh; and the like thereof in fabric: (A, and Har ubi suprà:) or ↓ zrby~p signifies [simply] a carpet ( TinofisapN ): and a carpet ( bisaAT ) having a nap, or pile: and a [ piece of leather that is spread upon the ground, such as is called ] niTaE : and the like thereof in make. (TA. [See also the last sentence of this paragraph.]) [Hence,] one says, AlbagoDaA='i bayonahumo mabovuwvapN ↓ zaraAbiY~u (tropical:) [ The embellished coverings of vehement hatred are spread between them; i. e. vehement hatred concealed by fair professions &c. subsists between them]. (A.) The following saying, of Artáh Ibn-Suheiyeh, wanaHonu banuw Eam~K EalaY *aAti bayoninaA fiyhaA bigoDapN watanAfusu ↓ zaraAbiY~u is expl. by En-Nemiree as meaning (assumed tropical:) [ And we are sons of a paternal uncle, but] upon our enmity is a comely covering beneath which it is latent; [ therein are vehement hatred and envious competition; ] zaraAbiY~u signifying [properly] carpets of sundry colours: (Ham p. 196:) it is also said to mean, in this instance, (assumed tropical:) [ concealed ] enmities, and sayings that give pain; [the former of these two meanings being] from zarabotu Albahoma fiY Alz~ariybapi , i. e. A^adoxalotuhu : [the latter of them app. suggested by another reading, namely, zaA^aAnibu in the place of zaraAbiY~u ; mentioned and thus explained in the Ham ubi suprà: the poet, therefore, is supposed to have meant, upon our state of union, or concord, ( *At bynnA having two contr. significations,) have supervened concealed enmities, &c.:] or, as some say, the reading in the deewán of Artáh is zaraAy^ibu , as though pl. of ↓ zariybapN , which is likewise made to denote enmity because it is made to enter ( tuzorabu , i. e. tudoxalu ,) into the heart; or which may be metaphorically applied to a place of enmity latent in the bosom, from the same word as signifying the “ place in which are put lambs, or kids, and sheep, or goats: ” or, supposing the right reading to be ↓ zaraAbiY~u , the poet may very properly mean, upon the vacant space between our tents, or houses, are carpets ( TanaAfis and busuT ) spread for us, and we sit thereon, near together in the places, but with the hearts remote: (idem p. 195:) but with the reading zaA^aAnibu , mentioned above, occurs another variation, thus: EalaY *aAka bayonanaA zaA^aAnibu ; meaning, notwithstanding that, between us are sayings that give pain. (Idem p. 196.) ― -b2- ↓ wayolN lilz~arobiy~api , occurring in a trad., is said to mean (tropical:) Wo to those who go in to lords, or princes, and, when they say what is evil, or say anything, say, He has spoken truth: such persons being likened, in respect of their variable conduct, to one of the zaraAbiY~ mentioned above in the first sentence of this paragraph; or to sheep, or goats, which are thus called in relation to the zarob , i. e. the enclosure to which they repair, because they are obsequious to the lords, or princes, and follow their steps with the submissiveness of sheep or goats to their pastor. (TA.) ― -b3- Accord. to El-Muärrij, (TA,) ↓ zaraAbiY~u is applied to plants, as meaning Such as have become yellow, or red, while having in them greenness: (K, TA:) and when they saw the colours in carpets and other articles of furniture that are spread, they likened them to such plants. (TA.)

(MA, KL, PS: [and the like is indicated in the S and Msb and K.]) [ zaAnahu said of a quality, and of an action, and of a saying, is best rendered It adorned him, or graced him, or was an honour to him; contr. of $aAnahu ; as is indicated in the S and K: and sometimes means it was his pride: and ↓ zy~nhu means as expl. above: and he embellished it, dressed it up, or trimmed it; said in this sense as relating to language: and he embellished it, or dressed it up, namely, an action &c. to another ( ligayorihi ); often said in this sense of the Devil; (as in the Kur vi. 43, &c.;) i. e. he commended it to him:] zaAnahu ka*aA and ↓ zy~nhu [ Such a thing adorned him, &c.,] are expl. as said when one's excellence [ faDoluhu , as I read for fElh , an evident mistranscription,] appears either by speech or by action: and A@ll~`hi liloA^a$oyaA='i ↓ tazoyiynu [ God's adorning, &c., of things ] is sometimes by means of his creating them muzay~anap [i. e. adorned, &c.]; and Aln~aAsi ↓ tazoyiynu [ The adorning, &c., of men ], by their abundance of property, and by their speech, i. e. by their extolling Him. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , the subst. from zaAnahu , (Msb,) signifies maA yutazay~anu bihi [i. e. A thing with which, or by which, one is adorned, ornamented, decorated, decked, bedecked, garnished, embellished, beautified, or graced; or with which, or by which, one adorns, &c., himself ]; (T, S, K;) any such thing; (T, TA;) [ any ornament, ornature, decoration, garnish, embellishment, or grace; ] and so ↓ ziyAnN ; (K;) and ↓ zayonN , also, [which see above,] signifies the same as ziynapN : (Har p. 139:) accord. to El- Harállee, ziynapN denotes the [ means of ] beautifying, or embellishing, a thing by another thing; consisting of apparel, or an ornament of gold or silver or of jewels or gems, or aspect: or, as some say, it is the beauty [ seen ] of the eye that does not reach to the interior of that which is adorned [ thereby ]: accord. to Er-Rághib, its proper mean- ing is a thing that does not disgrace, or render unseemly, a man, in any of his states or conditions, either in the present world or in that which is to come: but that which adorns him in one state or condition, exclusively of another, is in one point of view $ayonN : summarily speaking, it is of three kinds; namely, mental, such as knowledge or science, and good tenets; and bodily, such as strength, and tallness of stature, and beauty of aspect; and extrinsic, such as wealth, and rank or station or dignity; and all these are mentioned in the Kur: (TA:) the pl. is ziyanN . (Bd in x. 25.) ziynapu AlHayaApi Ald~unoyaA [or simply ziynapu Ald~unoyaA generally means The ornature, finery, show, pomp, or gaiety, of the present life or world; and] particularly includes wealth and children. (Kur xviii. 44.) ziynapu AlA^aroDi [ The ornature of the earth ] means the plants, or herbage, of the earth. (TA.) yawomu Alz~iynapi [ The day of ornature ] is the festival ( AlEiydu ); (S, K;) when men used [and still use] to adorn themselves with goodly articles of apparel. (TA.) And also The day of the breaking [ of the dam a little within the entrance ] of the canal of Misr [here meaning the present capital of Egypt, El-Káhireh, which we call “ Cairo ”], (K, TA,) i. e. the canal which runs through the midst of Misr, and [the dam of] which is broken when the Nile has attained the height of sixteen cubits or more: this day is said to be meant in the Kur xx. 61: it is one of the days observed in Egypt with the greatest gladness and rejoicing from ancient times; and its observance in the days of the Fátimees was such as is inconceivable, as it is described in the “ Khitat ” of El-Makreezee. (TA. [The modern observances of this day, and of other days in relation to the rise of the Nile, are described in my work on the Modern Egyptians.])

definition: , (K,) inf. n. musaAjalapN , (S, IB, TA,) [and app. sijaAlN also, (see sajolN ,)] He vied, competed, or contended for superiority, with him; emulated, or rivalled, him; or imitated him; (S, IB, * K;)...
sourceDefinition: , (K,) inf. n. musaAjalapN , (S, IB, TA,) [and app. sijaAlN also, (see sajolN ,)] He vied, competed, or contended for superiority, with him; emulated, or rivalled, him; or imitated him; (S, IB, * K;) doing like as he did; (S, IB;) originally in the drawing of water; (S, * IB;) each of them bringing forth in his sajol [or bucket ] the like of what the other brought forth [or endeavouring to do so ]; the one, of them, that desisted being overcome: (IB:) and also, (assumed tropical:) in running: or in watering. (S.) Hence, fulaAnN yusaAjilu fulaAnFA (tropical:) Such a one vies with such a one, each of them producing, [ of the evidences ] of nobility, the like of what the other produces; the one, of them, that desists being overcome. (IB.) El-Fadl Ibn- 'Abbás Ibn-'Otbeh Ibn-Abee-Lahab says, mano yusaAjiloniY yusaAjilo maAjidFA yamolaA^u Ald~alowa A_ilaY Eaqodi Alkarabo [ He who contends for superiority with me contends for superiority with one possessing glory, who fills the bucket to the tying of the rope that is attacked to the middle of its cross-bars ]: and hence the saying, AlHarobu sijaAlN . (S. [See sajolN .])

definition: A full bucket: so accord.
sourceDefinition: A full bucket: so accord. to Az and ElFárábee and others: (MS:) or a bucket containing water, whether little or much: such as is empty is not called sajolN nor *anuwbN : (S:) or a great bucket: (Msb: [see also sajiylN :]) or a great bucket that is full (K, TA) of water: (TA:) and a bucketful; the quantity that fills a bucket: (K:) it is of the masc. gender [though dalowN (the most common word for “ a bucket ”) is generally fem.]: (S, K:) pl. sijaAlN . (S.) ― -b2- And [hence,] (assumed tropical:) A share, or portion; (Msb;) like dalaApN [which likewise originally signifies “ a bucket ”]. (S in art. dlw . [See also sajiylN .]) And hence is derived the saying, AlHarobu sijaAlN , [as though meaning (assumed tropical:) War is an affair of shares, or portions; ] i. e. the victory in war is shared by turns among the people [engaged therein]: (Msb:) [but it is implied in the S that it is from AlmusaAjalapu , and that sijaAlN is here an inf. n. like musaAjalapN , agreeably with analogy; and if so, the saying may be rendered war is a contention for superiority: (see 3:)] or the saying AlHarobu bayonahumo sijaAlN means (assumed tropical:) [ War between them consists of portions, in such a manner that ] a sajol [or portion ] thereof is against these, and another is against these: (K:) originating from the act of two men drawing water with two buckets from a well, each of them having [in his turn] a full bucket. (TA.) You say also, A^aEoTaAhu sajolahu mino ka*aA (tropical:) He gave him his share, or portion, of such a thing; like as one says, *anuwbahu . (Har p. 19.) The phrase sajolN ↓ sajiylN in the saying lahumo mina Almajodi sajolN sajiylN (K, * TA) has an intensive signification; (K, TA;) [the saying app. meaning (assumed tropical:) They have, of glory, a large share. ] ― -b3- Hence likewise, metaphorically applied to signify (tropical:) A gift: one says jawaAdN EaZiymu Als~ajoli (tropical:) [ A bountiful man who is large in gift ]. (Har ibid. [The first word in this saying is there written jw~Ad .]) One says also, lahu bir~N faAy^iDu Als~ijaAli (assumed tropical:) [ He has overflowing goodness or beneficence ]. (TA.) ― -b4- Also (assumed tropical:) A bountiful man. (Abu-l-' Omeythil, K.) ― -b5- And (assumed tropical:) A great udder: pl. sijaAlN and sujuwlN . (K.) -A2- See also sijil~N , in two places.

definition: A writing; or paper, or piece of skin, written upon; (K, * TA;) as also sujul~N (TA) and ↓ sijolN (K, TA) [and ↓ sajolN , as appears from what follows]: or a TuwmaAr [meaning a roll, or scroll, or...
sourceDefinition: A writing; or paper, or piece of skin, written upon; (K, * TA;) as also sujul~N (TA) and ↓ sijolN (K, TA) [and ↓ sajolN , as appears from what follows]: or a TuwmaAr [meaning a roll, or scroll, or the like, ] for writing upon or written upon: (Bd in xxi. 104:) and a written statement of a contract and the like; (K, TA;) i. e. (TA) i. q. Sak~N : (S, TA: [but see this word, which has also other meanings, and among them that here following, which is the most common meaning of sijil~N :]) the record of a kádee, or judge, in which his sentence is written; (Msb;) a judicial record: (Mgh:) [see also maHoDarN :] pl. sijil~aAtN . (Msb, K.) kaTaY~i Als~ijil~i lilokitaAbi , in the Kur xxi. 104, means Like the folding of the TuwmaAr [expl. above] for the purpose of writing [thereon]: or for what is to be written: (Bd:) or upon what is written; (Bd, * Jel;) i. e., upon the written record [of the works] of the son of Adam at his death: (Jel:) or Als~ijil~ here has the third of the meanings here following: (Bd, Jel:] or the second thereof. (Bd.) ― -b2- And A writer, or scribe: (K:) and so some explain it in the verse above cited. (TA.) ― -b3- And Als~ijil~u A certain scribe of the Prophet. (K.) ― -b4- And A certain angel, (K,) who folds the written statements of [ men's ] works. (Bd ubi suprà.) ― -b5- And, without the article, A man, in the Abyssinian language. (K.) In the verse cited above, I' Ab read ↓ Als~ajoli , and explained it as meaning A certain man: but it is also said to mean a certain angel: and another reading is Als~ujul~i , a dial. var. mentioned above. (TA.)

definition: Stones like lumps of dry, or tough, clay: arabicized from sanoG wa Gilo ;
sourceDefinition: Stones like lumps of dry, or tough, clay: arabicized from sanoG wa Gilo ; (K, TA;) which are Pers. words, meaning “ stone and clay; ” the conjunction falling out in the arabicizing: (TA:) or baked clay: (Jel in xi. 84 and xv. 74 and cv. 4:) or stones (S, K) of clay (S) baked by the fire of Hell, whereon were inscribed the names of the people [ for whom they were destined ]: (S, K:) so in the Kur; as is indicated therein, in li. 33 and 34: (S:) or mino saj~iylK in the Kur means mino sijil~K , i. e. of what had been written [or decreed ] for them, that they should be punished therewith; and sij~iyl means the same as sij~iyn , mentioned and expl. in the Kur lxxxiii. 8 and 9: (K:) AO says that mn sj~yl means many and hard; and that sij~iynN is syn. with sij~iylN in this sense: (TA:) it is also said to be from sij~iynN meaning Hell; the n being changed into l : (Bd in xi. 84:) also, to be from A^asojalotuhu meaning “ I sent forth him or it: ” or from A^asojalotu meaning “ I gave; ” and to be from Als~ajolu . (TA.) -A2- Also i. q. daAy^imN ; and so sij~iyno [q. v.]. (L in art. sjn .)

definition: Allowed, or made allowable, to every one;
sourceDefinition: Allowed, or made allowable, to every one; (S, K;) not denied to any one. definition: , (S, M, Mgh, K,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, M, Mgh, K,) aor. yasoruw ; (S, K;) and saraA , (S, M, K,) aor. as above; (S, K;) and sariYa , (S, M, K,) aor. yasoraY ; (S, K;) inf. n. saraAwapN , (S, M, K,) of the first verb, (S, M,) and sarowN , (Sb, Lh, S, M, Mgh, K,) of the same verb, (M, Mgh,) and of the second, (S, M,) and of the third, (S,) and sarFA and saraA='N , (M, K,) both of the third, but saraA='N , and this only, is mentioned by Lh as inf. n. of the second verb; (M;) He was, or became, possessed of liberality, bountifulness, munificence, or generosity, combined with manliness, or manly virtue: (S, Mgh:) or manliness, or manly virtue, (M, K,) and (M,) or combined with, (K,) high or elevated rank or condition, nobility, dignity, honour, or glory. (M, K.) -A2- sarowu AlmasaAqiY means The cleaning out of what are termed masaAqK [pl. of masoqaApN or misoqaApN , which see in art. sqY ]. (TA.) -A3- sarowN also signifies, like tasoriyapN [inf. n. of ↓ sr~Y ], and A_isoraA='N [inf. n. of ↓ AsrY ], The throwing off a thing from oneself [or from another]; (K, TA;) and the pulling off a thing. (TA.) You say, sarawotu Alv~awoba Ean~iY , (ISk, S,) or Eanohu , aor. A^asoruw , (Mgh,) inf. n. sarowN , I threw off the garment from me, (ISk, S,) or I removed the garment from over him; (Mgh;) and sarayotu is a dial. var. thereof; (S;) or saraA vawobahu Eanohu , inf. n. sarowN ; and ↓ sr~Ahu ; he pulled off his garment from him: (M:) and sarawotu Aljul~a Eani Alfarasi , (TA,) or Eano Zahori Alfarasi , (M,) and ↓ sar~ayotuhu , and ↓ A^asorayotuhu , I threw off [ the horse-cloth from the horse, or from the back of the horse ]. (TA.) And sarawotu Ean~iY diroEiY [ I threw off from me my coat of mail ]: in this case the verb is only with w . (S.) [Hence,] Eanohu ↓ sur~iYa , (M,) or sur~iYa Eanohu Alham~u , (S, K, *) inf. n. tasoriyapN , (TA,) (tropical:) Anxiety became removed from him; as also Eanohu ↓ AnsrY Alham~u : (S, K, * TA:) or his anxiety became removed, or cleared away. definition: , as an epithet applied to a man, (S, M, K, &c.
sourceDefinition: , as an epithet applied to a man, (S, M, K, &c.,) may be from Aisotarayotu Al$~aYo'a “ I chose, or selected, the thing, ” or from Als~araApu “ the higher, or highest, part ” of a thing, (Ham p. 337,) or, accord. to Er-Rághib, from sarawotu Alv~awoba Ean~iY “ I pulled off the garment from me, ” (TA, [in which this derivation is said to be good, but I think it far-fetched,]) Possessing liberality, bountifulness, munificence, or generosity, combined with manliness, or manly virtue: (S, Mgh:) or possessing manliness, or manly virtue, (M, K,) and, (M,) or combined with, (K,) high or elevated rank or condition, nobility, dignity, honour, or glory: (M, K:) or i. q. ray^iysN [meaning a chief, or person high in rank or condition ]: (Msb:) [or a generous and manly or noble person:] fem. with p : (M, K:) and ↓ masorawaAnN signifies the same, applied to a man; and ↓ masorawaAnapN applied to a woman: (M:) the pl. of sariY~N is A^asoriyaA='u and surawaA='u (Lh, M, K) and surFY , (Az, K,) which is anomalous, (TA,) and saraApN , (T, S, Mgh, * Msb,) [originally sarawapN ,] which is [also] anomalous, (T, TA,) the only instance of faEalapN as the measure of a pl. of a word of the measure faEiylN , (S, Msb,) or it is a quasi-pl. n., (Sb, M, K,) and its pl. is sarawaAtN ; (S, M, Mgh, * K;) meaning saAdaAtN [or chiefs, &c.]; (Mgh); and suraApN , with damm, [originally surawapN ,] is a dial. var. of saraApN , as pl. [or quasi-pl. n.] of sariY~N : (IAth, TA:) the pl. of sariy~apN is sariy~aAtN and saraAyaA . (M, K.) Also Chosen, or choice, or select: (M:) what is good of anything; pl. [or quasi-pl. n.] saraApN : (Ham p. 337:) the best, (Msb, TA, and Har p. 56,) and in like manner saraApN [as a pl.]; (M, Msb, TA, and Ham p. 57, and Har ubi suprà;) the former, of men, (Har ubi suprà,) and of camels; (S;) and the latter, of men, (S, TA, and Ham ubi suprà, and Har,) and of cattle or camels and the like, (S, M, TA,) as also the former. (TA.) -A2- See also art. srY .

(Mgh.)

definition: , or sukur~ajapN , accord.
sourceDefinition: , or sukur~ajapN , accord. to different authorities, (TA,) or both, (MF,) not an Arabic word, but occurring in a trad.; [arabicized from the Pers. sukoraJahN , meaning A saucer; ] a sort of small bowl-shaped vessel, in [or out of ] which one eats: it is of two sizes; the larger holding six ounces; and the smaller, three ounces, or four mithkáls, or between two thirds of an ounce [ and some other quantity more or less (for there is an omission in this place in my original)]: in such vessels, placed upon the tables, around the meats, the Arabs used to put sauces and the like to excite the appetite and to aid digestion: expl. by Ed-Dáwoodee as a small, varnished, bowlshaped vessel. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: (Sh, S, M, Msb, K, &c.) and ↓ A^usokuwfN (Sh, S, M, K) and ↓ A^asokafN and ↓ sak~aAfN and ↓ sayokafN (K) A maker of boots, (Sh, Msb, K,) or of shoes or sandals; (MA;) or a sewer of boots &c.: (Msb;) or the first word, (Msb, K, TA,) as used by the Arabs [of the desert], (Msb, TA,) any artificer, or artisan, (Msb, K, TA,) thus expl. in the M, and so its three [perhaps a mistake for four] dial. vars., but said by J [in the S] to be a meaning not known, (TA,) except the maker of boots, for he is called ↓ A^asokafN , (K, TA,) i. e. when they mean such as is called A_isokaAfN in the cities or towns or villages: (TA:) or a carpenter; (K;) in which sense it is used by Esh-Shemmákh, but J says, [in the S,] only on the ground of supposition; (TA;) and any handicraftsman who works with an iron tool: (AA, K, * TA:) pl. A^asaAkifapN (S, Msb, TA) [and A^asaAkiyfu ]. ― -b2- Also the first word, Skilful with an affair. (O, K.) Sh says, I heard El-Fak'asee say, A_in~aka lA_isokaAfN bih`*aA AlA^amori , meaning Verily thou art skilful with this affair. (O.) -A2- Accord. to Ibn-'Abbád, AlA_isokaAfu is also used (O, K) by Ibn-Mukbil (O) as meaning The redness of wine: but this is a mistranscription, (O, K,) and a perversion of the meaning: (O:) the right word is AlA_isokaAb . (O, K.)

sourceDefinition: , [aor. ,] inf. n. salaAmapN (S, M, A, Mgh, Msb, K) and salaAmN (A, TA) and salamN and salomN and silomN , (Bd in xxxix. 30,) He was, or became, safe, or secure; or he escaped; (M, TA;) or he was, or became, free; (TA;) mina AlA=faAti [ from evils of any kind ], (S, Mgh,) or mina AlA=fapi [ from evil of any kind ], (K,) or mina AlbalaA='i [ from trial, or affliction ], (A, TA,) or mina AlA^amori [ from the affair ]: (M:) he (a traveller) was, or became, safe, secure, or free, from evils of any kind: (Msb:) and salima mina AlEayobi he was, or became, free from fault, defect, imperfection, blemish, or vice; syn. bariy^a . (Msb in art. brA^ .) [Hence,] one says, laA bi*iY tasolamu maA kaAna Ga*aA waka*aA , (ISk, S, K, *) meaning No, by God [or Him ] who maketh thee to be in safety, (ISk, S, K,) [ such and such things were not; ] and to two persons lA b*Y tasolamaAni , and to a pl. number lA b*Y tasolamuwna , and to a female lA b*Y tasolamiyna , and to a pl. number [of females] lA b*Y tasolamona . (ISk, S, K. *) And laA A^afoEalu *`lika bi*iY tasolamu , meaning, bi*iY salaAmatiki [i. e. I will not do that, by the Author (lit. Lord or Master ) of thy safety ]; and in like manner, b*Y tasolamaAni , and b*Y tasolamuwna . (Sb, M. [See also *w .]) And Ai*ohabo bi*iY tasolamu , i. e. Ai*ohabo bisalaAmatika [ Go thou with thy safety; or, with the Author of thy safety to protect thee; meaning go thou in safety ]; and [to two persons] Ai*ohabaA bi*iY tasolamaAni . (S, K.) *Y is thus prefixed to a verb [as virtually governing it in the gen. case] like as A=yap is in an instance mentioned under this latter word; but these are two extr. instances; for only a noun significant of time is [regularly] prefixed to a verb, as in the phrase h`*aA yawomu yufoEalu , meaning yufoEalu fiyhi : (Akh, S:) it is not prefixed to any but this verb tasolamu [and its variations as above mentioned]. (Sb, M, K.) ― -b2- And hence, (Mgh,) one says also, salimato lahu AlD~ayoEapu , meaning [ The landed estate ] was, or became, free from participation to him; syn. xalaSat . (Mgh, TA.) -A2- slmhu , [app. salamahu , or perhaps salimahu , for some verbs of this measure are trans., as Hasiba and wariva ,] inf. n. slm , [app. salamN , q. v. infrà,] He made him a captive. (TA.) -A3- salamatohu AlHay~apu , (TA,) inf. n. salomN , (M, K, TA,) The serpent bit him: (M, * K, * TA:) mentioned by Az, but he adds that no one but Lth has said this. (TA.) -A4- salama Aljiloda , aor. , (S, K,) inf. n. salomN , (TA,) He tanned the skin with [ qaraZ , i. e. leaves of ] the salam [or mimosa flava ]. (S, K, TA.) ― -b2- salama Ald~alowa , (M, K,) aor. , inf. n. salomN , (M,) He finished making the leathern bucket; and made it firm, strong, or sound, or made it firmly, strongly, or soundly. (M, K.)

definition: , (S, M, Msb, K,) inf.
sourceDefinition: , (S, M, Msb, K,) inf. n. tasoliymN , (K,) He (God) made him to be safe, secure, or free; saved, secured, or freed, him; (M, Msb, TA;) mina AlA=faAti [ from evils of any kind ], (S, Msb,) or mina AlA=fapi [ from evil of any kind ], (K,) or mina AlA^amori [ from the affair ]. (M.) [Freytag assigns the same meaning to ↓ Aslmhu also, as on the authority of the Ham; in which I find no explanation of this verb except one which will be found later in this paragraph.] ― -b2- [Hence,] Alt~asoliymu is also syn. with Als~alaAmu , (S, K, TA,) as meaning The saluting, or greeting, one with a prayer for his safety, or security, or freedom, from evils of any kind in his religion and in his person; and the interpretation thereof is [ the expressing a desire for ] Alt~axoliySN ; (Mbr, TA;) or the saluting, or greeting, one with a prayer for his life; or, by saying salaAmN Ealayoka [q. v. infrà, voce salaAmN ]; syn. Alt~aHiy~apu . (TA.) You say, sal~ama Ealayohi [meaning He so saluted, or greeted, him ]. (M, Msb.) [This, when said of God, virtually means sal~amahu , i. e. He saved him; and should be rendered agreeably with this explanation in the phrase commonly used after the mention of the Prophet, Sal~aY A@ll~`hu Ealayohi wasal~ama May God bless and save him. You say also, sal~ama Ealayohi biAlxilaAfapi He saluted him with the acknowledgment of his being Khaleefeh; saying, salaAmN Ealayoka yaA A^amiyra Almuw^ominiyna Salutation to thee, or peace be on thee, &c., O Prince of the Faithful. ] Alt~asoliymapu signifies The salutation that is pronounced on finishing every two rek'ahs in prayer: (Har p. 180:) [and also that which is pronounced after the last rek'ah of each of the prayers (i. e. after the sunneh prayers and the fard alike), addressed to the two guardian and recording angels: (see my “ Modern Egyptians, ” ch. iii., p. 78 of the 5th ed.:) and sal~ama means He pronounced either of those salutations. ] ― -b3- [Hence also,] sl~m A_ilayohi Al$~aYo'a , (S, K, *) inf. n. as above; (K;) and ↓ Aslm Alyh Al$Y'a ; (M;) He gave to him the thing; (S, * M, K;) or delivered it to him: (M:) [ he resigned it to him: ] and sl~m A_ilayohi AlwadiyEapa , (Mgh,) or sl~m AlwadiyEapa liSaAHibihaA , He delivered the deposit [ to him, or] to its owner: (Msb:) and ↓ Aslm Alv~awoba A_ilaY Alxay~aATi (Mgh) signifies the same as sl~mhu A_ilayohi [i. e. He delivered the garment, or piece of cloth, to the tailor ]. (Har p. 166.) ― -b4- See also 4, in two places. ― -b5- You say also, sl~m AlA^ajiyru nafosahu lilomusotaA^ojiri The hired man gave himself up, or gave authority over himself, to the hirer. (Msb.) And ↓ A^asolamotuhu and sal~amotuhu I left him in the power of him who desired to kill him or to wound him. (Ham p. 115.)
